info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.

A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

Use the tools to answer the question: Context: we are developing an inexpensive, open-source, gravimetric powder doser (auger / vibratory feed with a load-cell balance in the loop) for self-driving laboratories. It was designed for multi-powder dosing of metal powders for additive-manufacturing alloy discovery and targets the milligram-to-gram range; it is not intended for sub-milligram dosing. We want to know where it could be useful in drug discovery, in particular as the upstream 'weigh solid into a vial, then dissolve' step that precedes far smaller (nanoliter-to-picoliter) liquid dispensing onto microplates or lab-on-a-chip / organ-on-chip devices. Review the current technology for automated milligram- and gram-scale solid/powder dispensing used in pharmaceutical research and drug discovery: gravimetric dosing heads and platforms (Mettler Toledo Quantos and CHRONECT XPR, Chemspeed GDU-S SWILE / GDU-Pfd / FLEX / SWING / Crystal Powderdose, Unchained Labs (Freeslate) Junior and Big Kahuna, Zinsser Analytic, Labman, Symyx Powdernium, Sartorius, Hamilton, Brooks/Titian, Tecan), positive-displacement solid dispensers (e.g. SWILE), capsule micro-dosers for API-in-capsule (Capsugel Xcelodose, 3P Innovation Fill2Weigh), and alternative strategies (ChemBeads / coated-bead solid dispensing, dissolve-and-dispense stock-solution workarounds, vibratory / tapping / sieving micro-feeders, electrostatic or acoustic powder dosing). For each, report dose range, accuracy and %RSD (especially at 0.1-1 mg, 1-5 mg, 5-50 mg and gram targets), dispense time, dependence on powder properties (cohesive, electrostatic, hygroscopic, needle-shaped APIs; Hausner ratio, flow function), containment of potent compounds (OEB / OEL), cross-contamination and cleaning, and approximate cost. Include the multi-company benchmarking studies of automated powder dispensing in pharma high-throughput experimentation (e.g. Bahr et al. 2018 and 2020) and any newer 2021-2026 evaluations, plus open-source or low-cost academic powder dispensers built for self-driving labs. Provide a comparison table and full citations with DOIs.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll create a comprehensive plan to address this detailed question about automated powder dispensing technologies in pharmaceutical research.

Abstract:
Pharmaceutical tablet formulation and process development, traditionally a complex and multi-dimensional decision-making process, necessitates extensive experimentation and resources, often resulting in suboptimal solutions. This study presents an integrated platform for tablet formulation and manufacturing, built around a Digital Formulator and a Self-Driving Tableting DataFactory. By combining predictive modelling, optimisation algorithms, and automation, this system offers a material-to-product approach to predict and optimise critical quality attributes for different formulations, linking raw material attributes to key blend and tablet properties, such as flowability, porosity, and tensile strength. The platform leverages the Digital Formulator, an in-silico optimisation framework that employs a hybrid system of models - melding data-driven and mechanistic models - to identify optimal formulation settings for manufacturability. Optimised formulations then proceed through the self-driving Tableting DataFactory, which includes automated powder dosing, tablet compression and performance testing, followed by iterative refinement of process parameters through Bayesian optimisation methods. This approach accelerates the timeline from material characterisation to development of an in-specification tablet within 6 hours, utilising less than 5 grams of API, and manufacturing small batch sizes of up to 1,440 tablets with augmented and mixed reality enabled real-time quality control within 24 hours. Validation across multiple APIs and drug loadings underscores the platform's capacity to reliably meet target quality attributes, positioning it as a transformative solution for accelerated and resource-efficient pharmaceutical development.

Abstract:
Objectives Liquid medications provide an alternative to splitting pills and dosages by measuring an amount of liquid rather than crushing tablets or opening capsules. Special attention should also be paid to specific patient groups with swallowing difficulties or requiring enteral feeding administration. Liquid medicines are also often used to ease withdrawal symptoms for people suffering from addiction. Nevertheless, filling liquid medication cups with the right medication and precise doses may be difficult for healthcare professionals. The Nooddis (‘Nominative Oral Dose Dispenser’—Pierre Lôo Hospital, France and Packinov, France) is a new robotic system for the automated filling of single dose liquid medications. Since the performance of such a complex piece of equipment depends on compliance of the service provider to our building guidelines, the process performance verification is a necessary prerequisite before starting routine production. Methods The performance of the Nooddis robot (accuracy, precision, and tapering calculation) and its ability to fill medicine cups was evaluated with 18 different liquid medications using an automatic in-line checkweigher. Microbiological testing was also performed. Results 648 sealed cups were prepared for qualification. The filling accuracy was within the limit of ±10% from 75 µL to 21.25 mL. The repeatability (% relative SD (%RSD) 0.05 to 4.93) and intermediate precision (%RSD 0.01 to 6.59) were validated for all preparations. All medicine cups met the requirements of USP and European Pharmacopoeia acceptance criteria for microbiological quality. Automated tapering calculations allowed for easy production of daily doses for the tapering periods chosen. Conclusion Since the system met the required quality standards, the Nooddis robot, with automatic in-line tapering system, is regarded as an accurate technology that can fill the exact amount of liquid oral medication in single dose cups. This may promote closer monitoring, which supports medication tapering as well as medication misuse prevention. With a packaging cost similar to current unit dose cup systems, it is a relevant alternative to fractioned or crushed tablets, as well as opened capsules. Further developments for some sterile liquid medications are yet to be studied.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Solid sampling at the sub-milligram and milligram scale remains a major bottleneck for high-throughput chemistry or material sciences, as existing approaches rely on manual handling or slow deterministic microsampling that do not readily scale. Here we present STORMS, an automated STOchastic Robotic MicroSampling system that enables fast, reliable and parallel sampling of solid materials at sub-milligram and milligram masses. Rather than attempting deterministic mass control, STORMS leverages stochastic sampling combined with robotic automation, and glass encapsulation to achieve statistically robust and reproducible sample collection. We show that this approach delivers high precision and throughput across a range of solid materials, while supporting straightforward parallelization thanks to encapsulation and minimal operator intervention. Benchmarking against conventional sampling workflows demonstrates substantial gains in speed and reproducibility. By decoupling sampling reliability from deterministic mass control, STORMS establishes stochastic microsampling as a general and scalable strategy for solid analysis at the sub-milligram and milligram scale.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Exploration of synthetic transformations using high throughput experimentation (HTE) can accelerate the rapid discovery of optimal conditions for organic reactions and improve our understanding of those processes and synthetic route for different applications. The surge in high throughput techniques has been applied to a broad range of methods and target-oriented reaction optimizations across a diverse array of bond-constructions. In this Minireview, we describe HTE based workflows, discuss different transformations that have been evaluated using HTE platforms with a focus on homogeneous catalytic reactions, and highlight challenges reported in the field since 2016. The HTE efforts are grouped by the type of bonds being formed, for instance, carbon-carbon (C-C), carbon-nitrogen (C-N), carbon-halogen or carbon-oxygen (C-X) bonds, as well as photochemical transformations and hydrogenations. The potential of HTE to rapidly guide the optimization of multiple synthetic challenges makes it a very attractive and powerful tool for synthetic organic chemists.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>High‐throughput experimentation (HTE), the miniaturization and parallelization of reactions, is a valuable tool for accelerating diverse compound library generation, optimizing reaction conditions, and enabling data collection for machine learning (ML) applications. When applied to organic synthesis and methodology, HTE still poses various challenges due to the diverse workflows and reagents required, motivating advancements in reaction design, execution, analysis, and data management. To address these limitations, cutting‐edge technologies, automation, and artificial intelligence (AI) have been implemented to standardize protocols, enhance reproducibility, and improve efficiency. Additionally, strategies to reduce bias and promote serendipitous discoveries have further strengthened HTE's impact. This review highlights recent advances at every stage of the HTE workflow, including the development of customized workflows, diverse analysis, and improved data management practices for greater accessibility and shareability. Furthermore, we examine the current state of the field, outstanding challenges, and future directions toward transforming HTE into a fully integrated, flexible, and democratized platform that drives innovation in organic synthesis.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Automation has become an increasingly popular tool for synthetic chemists over the past decade. Recent advances in robotics and computer science have led to the emergence of automated systems that execute common laboratory procedures including parallel synthesis, reaction discovery, reaction optimization, time course studies, and crystallization development. While such systems offer many potential benefits, their implementation is rarely automatic due to the highly specialized nature of synthetic procedures. Each reaction category requires careful execution of a particular sequence of steps, the specifics of which change with different conditions and chemical systems. Careful assessment of these critical procedural requirements and identification of the tools suitable for effective experimental execution are key to developing effective automation workflows. Even then, it is often difficult to get all the components of an automated system integrated and operational. Data flows and specialized equipment present yet another level of challenge. Unfortunately, the pain points and process of implementing automated systems are often not shared or remain buried deep in the SI. This perspective provides an overview of the current state of automation of synthetic chemistry at the benchtop scale with a particular emphasis on core considerations and the ensuing challenges of deploying a system. Importantly, we aim to reframe automation as decidedly not automatic but rather an iterative process that involves a series of careful decisions (both human and computational) and constant adjustment.

Abstract:
Autonomous experimentation driven by artificial intelligence (AI) provides an exciting opportunity to revolutionize inorganic materials discovery and development. Herein, we review recent progress in the design of self-driving laboratories, including robotics to automate materials synthesis and characterization, in conjunction with AI to interpret experimental outcomes and propose new experimental procedures. We focus on efforts to automate inorganic synthesis through solution-based routes, solid-state reactions, and thin film deposition. In each case, connections are made to relevant work in organic chemistry, where automation is more common. Characterization techniques are primarily discussed in the context of phase identification, as this task is critical to understand what products have formed during synthesis. The application of deep learning to analyze multivariate characterization data and perform phase identification is examined. To achieve "closed-loop" materials synthesis and design, we further provide a detailed overview of optimization algorithms that use active learning to rationally guide experimental iterations. Finally, we highlight several key opportunities and challenges for the future development of self-driving inorganic materials synthesis platforms.

Abstract:
Introduction Rivaroxaban is an anticoagulant medication that targets a key stage in the blood clotting process, preventing the formation and growth of clots. It is commonly used to prevent thrombosis or inhibit the enlargement of existing clots. Rivaroxaban functions as a Factor Xa inhibitor and is indicated for reducing the risk of stroke and systemic embolism in patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation, treating deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE), as well as reducing the risk of recurrent DVT and PE, and prophylaxis of DVT, which may lead to PE in patients undergoing knee or hip replacement surgery. Methods A robust, precise, and selective reversed-phase high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) method was developed and validated for analyzing Rivaroxaban in raw materials. Isocratic elution at a flow rate of 1 mL/min was performed using a Thermo ODS Hypersil C18 column (4.6 × 250 mm, 5 µm) at ambient temperature. The mobile phase consisted of monobasic potassium phosphate at pH 2.9 and acetonitrile in a 70:30 (v/v) ratio, with UV detection at 249 nm. Results Linearity was established in the concentration range of 50–1,000 ppm (R2 = 0.999), and the retention time for Rivaroxaban was approximately 12 min. The percentage relative standard deviation (RSD) for precision and accuracy was consistently below 2.0%, ensuring method reliability. Solution stability studies confirmed the stability of Rivaroxaban over the analysis period, as no peak loss, degradation, or additional peaks were observed between the first and last injections. Furthermore, forced degradation studies were conducted under various stress conditions, including acid and base hydrolysis, as well as hydrogen peroxide oxidation. The method successfully resolved Rivaroxaban from its degradation products, demonstrating its stability-indicating capability. Conclusion Rivaroxaban is a novel oral anticoagulant that selectively and directly inhibits factor Xa. A method has been developed and validated for its analysis, adhering to guidelines from the International Conference on Harmonisation (ICH) and the U.S. Pharmacopeia (USP). The validation process assessed parameters such as specificity, robustness, linearity, accuracy, precision, limit of detection (LOD), and limit of quantitation (LOQ). The LOD for impurities and degradants was determined to be 0.3 ppm, while the LOQ was 1 ppm. This stability-indicating method is highly suitable for routine quality control and analytical applications in both raw materials and finished drug products, owing to its simplicity, efficiency, and robustness.

Abstract:
<jats:p>In iterative optimization, actions are adjusted based on what we see—such as dosing until dissolution or stirring until mixing is complete. Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) offer an opportunity to guide experimental adjustments based on such visual feedback in an autonomous, iterative way. However, current SDLs do not monitor these visual cues. HeinSight 4.0 fills this gap by integrating computer vision into SDLs to enable real-time experimental adjustments based on visual feedback. The computer vision detects equipment (e.g., reactor, vial), classifies chemical phases (solid, liquid, air), and analyzes image features such as turbidity and color. HeinSight 4.0 tracks these physical characteristics frame by frame and interprets physical states (e.g., dissolution, separation). This data feeds into a rule-based system that integrates with the SDL to make real-time experimental adjustments. We demonstrate HeinSight 4.0 adaptability across two pharmaceutical case studies: purification (solubility screening) and drug formulation (melt spray congeal). We also developed a hardware-agnostic architecture and deployed it across two institutions with distinct robotic systems. The open-source HeinSight 4.0 enables SDLs to see, think, and act in real time.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>This review proposes the concept of a “frugal twin,” similar to a digital twin, but for physical experiments. Frugal twins range from simple toy examples to low-cost surrogates of high-cost research. For example, a color-mixing self-driving laboratory (SDL) is a low-cost version of a costly multi-step chemical discovery SDL. We need frugal twins because they provide hands-on experience, a test bed for software prototyping (e.g., optimization, data infrastructure), and a low barrier to entry for democratizing SDLs. However, there is room for improvement. The true value of frugal twins can be realized in three core areas. Firstly, hardware and software modularity, secondly, purpose-built design (human-inspired vs. hardware-centric vs. human-in-the-loop), and thirdly state-of-the-art (SOTA) software (e.g., multi-fidelity optimization). We also describe the ethical benefits and risks that come with the democratization of science through frugal twins. In future work, we suggest ideas for new frugal twins, SDL educational course outcomes, and a classification scheme for autonomy levels.</jats:p>

Through the automation of experimental workflows, along with autonomous experimental planning, SDLs hold the potential to greatly accelerate research in chemistry and materials discovery. This review provides an in-depth analysis of the state-of-the-art in SDL technology, its applications across various scientific disciplines, and the potential implications for research and industry. This review additionally provides an overview of the enabling technologies for SDLs, including their hardware, software, and integration with laboratory infrastructure. The entire pharmaceutical sector is in an urgent need of both innovative technological solutions and fundamental scientific work, enabling the production of highly engineered drug products. Commercial‐scale manufacturing of complex drug delivery systems (DDSs) using the existing technologies is challenging. This review covers important elements of manufacturing sciences, beginning with risk management strategies and design of experiments (DoE) techniques. Experimental techniques should, where possible, be supported by computational approaches. With that regard, state‐of‐art mechanistic process modeling techniques are described in detail. Implementation of materials science tools paves the way to molecular‐based processing of future DDSs. A snapshot of some of the existing tools is presented. Additionally, general engineering principles are discussed covering process measurement and process control solutions. Last part of the review addresses future manufacturing solutions, covering continuous processing and, specifically, hot‐melt processing and printing‐based technologies. Abstract:
Capsule-based dry powder inhalers (cDPIs) are widely utilized in the delivery of pharmaceutical powders to the lungs. In these systems, the fundamental nature of the interactions between the drug/formulation powder, the capsules, the inhaler device, and the patient must be fully elucidated in order to develop robust manufacturing procedures and provide reproducible lung deposition of the drug payload. Though many commercially available DPIs utilize a capsule-based dose metering system, an in-depth analysis of the critical factors associated with the use of the capsule component has not yet been performed. This review is intended to provide information on critical factors to be considered for the application of a quality by design (QbD) approach for cDPI development. The quality target product profile (QTPP) defines the critical quality attributes (CQAs) which need to be understood to define the critical material attributes (CMA) and critical process parameters (CPP) for cDPI development as well as manufacturing and control.

This excerpt provides comparative data for three automated powder-dispensing platforms: a dual-arm robotic system, Mettler Toledo Quantos, and Chemspeed. The tested sodium nitrite target doses were 20, 200, 500, and 1000 mg, using a 2 mg tolerance. Dispense times (mean ± standard deviation, in seconds) were respectively 239 ± 30, 381 ± 73, 517 ± 72, and 552 ± 128 for the dual-arm robot; 285 ± 2, 31 ± 3, 33 ± 2, and 40 ± 4 for Quantos; and 62 ± 23, 109 ± 19, 132 ± 21, and 134 ± 17 for Chemspeed. The robot was therefore substantially slower, partly because it manipulated vials, hoppers, scale doors, spatulas, and other tools, and because correction cycles increased time. At a 200 mg target, non-challenging solids had errors below 2% for Quantos and the robot; the robot’s mean error was 0.07% with 0.56% standard deviation, versus Quantos −0.41% with 1.80%. Performance depended strongly on powder properties, target weight, and tolerance. Abrasive, hygroscopic, deliquescent, compressible, or sticky materials caused blockages, damaged dosing components, or dispensing failures. ## pqac-00000006

From text 'tu2026sticktothe pages 4-5'.

Noah P. Tu and Ying Wang. Stick to the beads: supercharging medicinal chemistry and methodology development with chembeads. RSC Medicinal Chemistry, 17:52-64, Jan 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1039/d5md00827a, doi:10.1039/d5md00827a. This article has 3 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

ChemBeads are chemically inert spherical glass beads coated with solid reagents to enable accurate, reproducible dispensing of very small quantities for high-throughput experimentation (HTE), including sub-milligram-scale dosing. Reagents are applied through dry particle coating, in which controlled mechanical force causes solid reagent particles to adhere uniformly to the glass-bead surface. Resonant acoustic mixing (RAM) is described as the most versatile and scalable coating method, with parameters such as mixing time, intensity, and bead-to-reagent ratio tunable for specific applications. After coating, vibratory sieving removes fines and aggregates, improves particle uniformity and flow, and helps prevent jamming in automated micro-dispensers. The resulting beads can be dispensed volumetrically by automated solid-dispensing robots into 96- or 384-well plates, or manually using calibrated fixed- or variable-volume scoops. A parallel dispenser uses calibrated metering holes to deliver beads efficiently into multiple receiving vials, combining low cost with higher throughput. The excerpt reports relative standard deviations typically below 5% for automated dispensing across 96-well formats and an error margin of ±5% for the parallel dispenser.

ChemBeads are a solid-handling technology in which active reagent powders are applied to chemically inert glass beads, converting poorly flowing solids into uniform, free-flowing materials that can be handled by robotic and manual dispensing systems. The approach was developed to address powder-to-powder differences in density, flowability, cohesiveness, and static behavior that caused weighing errors, instrument stalls, dose variability, cross-contamination, and irreproducible data in high-throughput experimentation. In preparation, the reagent is weighed precisely, selected beads are chosen according to factors such as surface area and size, and the finely powdered reagent is dry-mixed with the inert carrier. The reagent-to-bead loading is expressed as a weight-to-weight ratio or mmol g−1; the excerpt gives a typical range of 0.5–20%, with approximately 5% described as a versatile formulation that preserves flowability, homogeneity, and an appropriate dispense-weight range. Because the bead formulation standardizes physical handling properties while preserving chemical integrity, reagents can be dispensed volumetrically and reproducibly, similarly to liquids, using standard robotic bead-dispensing tools. The technology supports nanomole-to-milligram-scale dispensing with high accuracy and reproducibility, although the excerpt does not provide a specific numerical ChemBead accuracy or coefficient of variation.

ChemBeads are inert glass beads coated with solid reagents to enable rapid, small-scale, high-throughput experimentation (HTE) dispensing. The reagent is deposited physically on the bead surface, without chemical modification or covalent bonding, so the formulation retains the native reagent’s chemical properties and sensitivities. The excerpt describes calibrated fixed- or variable-volume scoops and a parallel ChemBead dispenser for transferring coated beads into 96-well screening plates. Multiple dispensers can add different reagents, while reagents may also be premixed before coating for simultaneous dispensing. The reported dispensing capability reaches reaction scales as low as 0.5 μmol per well; the excerpt does not provide a specific nanomole or sub-milligram accuracy figure. RAM instruments provide the most consistent and scalable dry-particle coating, whereas vortex mixing is functional but may be less consistent, lower-throughput, or less scalable. Accuracy and reproducibility depend on bead size, reagent properties, loading ratios, and preparation/storage conditions. Humidity, temperature, recrystallization, and reduced loading can impair performance. Standardized protocols and batch characterization can reduce variability, although complete inter-laboratory uniformity may remain difficult.

Abstract:
Highly potent active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and low-dose excipients, or excipients with very low density, are notoriously hard to feed with currently available commercial technology. The micro-feeder system presented in this work is capable of feeding low-dose rates of powders with different particle sizes and flow properties. Two different grades of lactose, di-calcium phosphate, croscarmellose sodium, silicon dioxide, a spray-dried intermediate, and an active ingredient were studied to vary material properties to test performance of the system. The current micro-feeder system is a volumetric feeder combined with a weighing balance at the outlet that measures feeder output rates. Feeding results are shown as a so-called “displacement-feed factor” curve for each material. Since the powder mass and volume are known in the micro-feeder system, in this work, we characterized an observed density variation during processing via a “displacement-feed factor” profile for each of the fed powders. This curve can be later used for calibrating the system to ensure an accurate, constant feed rate and in addition predicting feeding performance for that material at any feed rate. There is a relation between powder properties and feeding performance. Powders with finer particles and higher compressibility show densification during their feeding process. However, powders with larger particles and lower compressibility show both “densification” and “powder bed expansion,” which is the manifestation of dilation and elastic recovery of particles during the micro-feeding process. Through the application of the displacement-feed factor, it is possible to provide precise feeding accuracy of low-dose materials.

This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

STORMS is a stochastic, composition-centric robotic solid-dispensing system rather than a deterministic mass-targeting dispenser. It uses a UR3e six-axis collaborative robot (3 kg payload, 500 mm reach, ±0.03 mm repeatability) with a Robotiq Hand-E gripper (20–185 N grip-force range; approximately 0.025 mm repeatability), integrated with a vacuum-assisted solid-coring module and replaceable 316L stainless-steel tubes and rods. Samples are post-dispensing weighed, providing mass verification. The specified weighing instrument has 21 g capacity, 0.01 mg readability, and 0.01 mg repeatability, supporting sub-milligram samples down to approximately 0.1 mg; the excerpt does not provide a separate overall dispensing-accuracy or numerical throughput figure. Throughput is increased architecturally by accepting bounded mass deviations, correcting liquid composition downstream, and removing feedback-controlled dispensing from the critical path for parallel autonomous experimentation. Powder performance depends strongly on flowability, particle size, and cohesion: passive sampling is about 96% successful below a Carr index of 30 when particles fit inside the capillary, but falls to about 6% above 30. Hard granular salts require particles smaller than the capillary diameter. Highly cohesive powders form cavities because their surfaces do not re-level; vial-shaking strategies are being investigated to restore sampling performance.

Abstract:
3D-printed laboratory devices can enable ambitious research purposes even at a low-budget level. To follow this trend, here we describe the construction, calibration, and usage of the FINDUS (Fully Integrable Noncommercial Dispensing Utility System). We report the successful 3D printing and assembly of a liquid-handling workstation for less than $400. Using this setup, we achieve reliable and flexible liquid-dispensing automation with relative pipetting errors of less than 0.3%. We show our system is well suited for several showcase applications from both the biology and chemistry fields. In support of the open-source spirit, we make all 3D models, assembly instructions, and source code available for free download, rebuild, and modification.

## pqac-00000033

From text 'jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 10-10'.

Ying Jiang, Hatem Fakhruldeen, Gabriella Pizzuto, Louis Longley, Ai He, Tianwei Dai, Rob Clowes, Nicola Rankin, and Andrew I. Cooper. Autonomous biomimetic solid dispensing using a dual-arm robotic manipulator. Digital Discovery, 2:1733-1744, Jan 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1039/d3dd00075c, doi:10.1039/d3dd00075c. This article has 70 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides comparative accuracy data for three dispensing approaches—Quantos, the dual-arm robot, and Chemspeed—for thirteen solids at target weights of 20, 200, 500, and 1000 mg. Accuracy is reported as percentage error, apparently with a second value representing variability. The dual-arm robot generally shows small errors and relatively low variability for many materials and larger target weights. For example, at 1000 mg Al2O3, the listed errors are −0.02% for Quantos, 0.06% for the dual-arm robot, and −91.01% for Chemspeed; for pectin, the corresponding values are −0.01%, −0.04%, and −0.41%. Chemspeed also exhibits very large errors and variability for several materials, especially at lower weights, although performance varies by solid. Some entries show −100% error for all systems, indicating no successful dispensing for that material/condition, including NH4CH3CO2. The text attributes dispensing problems to a compressible solid clogging the spatula outlet. This excerpt does not provide throughput, dispensing time values, drug-discovery or formulation workflow outcomes, or purchase/operating costs for Chemspeed FLEX, SWING, Quantos, or other commercial systems. It therefore supports accuracy and failure-mode comparisons, but not cost or throughput comparisons.

## pqac-00000034

From text 'jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 10-11'.

Ying Jiang, Hatem Fakhruldeen, Gabriella Pizzuto, Louis Longley, Ai He, Tianwei Dai, Rob Clowes, Nicola Rankin, and Andrew I. Cooper. Autonomous biomimetic solid dispensing using a dual-arm robotic manipulator. Digital Discovery, 2:1733-1744, Jan 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1039/d3dd00075c, doi:10.1039/d3dd00075c. This article has 70 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt compares a dual-arm robotic dispensing platform with Mettler-Toledo Quantos and Chemspeed, using three overall performance metrics: range of solids dispensed, percentage error, and dispensing time. The dual-arm robot and Quantos handled a wider range of tested solids than Chemspeed. The dual-arm robot was more precise for non-challenging solids, but had longer dispensing times, indicating a throughput trade-off. Its principal advantage was versatility, including dispensing abrasive materials and solids with large particles, while it could restart a dispensing process when high absolute precision was required. The average dispensing failure rates reported in Table 7 were 23.1% for the dual-arm robot, 26.9% for Quantos, and 26.5% for Chemspeed. Chemspeed performed effectively with silicon carbide but had failures with sand and alumina; challenging materials varied by platform. Specific failures included calcium carbonate and ammonium acetate for the dual-arm robot, and hygroscopic or granular materials for other systems. The article notes that commercial systems may offer sub-milligram dispensing and larger cartridges, capabilities not available in the tested robotic system, as well as manual calibration for improved precision. The excerpt provides no purchase, lease, or operating costs for Chemspeed FLEX, SWING, Quantos, or other commercial systems, and does not give drug-discovery- or formulation-specific cost comparisons.

## pqac-00000035

From text 'tu2026sticktothe pages 4-5'.

Noah P. Tu and Ying Wang. Stick to the beads: supercharging medicinal chemistry and methodology development with chembeads. RSC Medicinal Chemistry, 17:52-64, Jan 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1039/d5md00827a, doi:10.1039/d5md00827a. This article has 3 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports that ChemBeads are compatible with automated solid-dispensing systems used in high-throughput experimentation (HTE), including Chemspeed Crystal Powderdose, Chemspeed Swile, Mettler Toledo Quantos, and Unchain Labs Junior. Initial studies with the Chemspeed SWAVE system achieved accurate and reproducible volumetric dispensing, with relative standard deviations typically below 5% across 96-well formats and sub-milligram accuracy. A customized automated robot is described as capable of reliable volumetric dosing into both 96- and 384-well microtiter plates, with a graphical user interface and protocol traceability. The systems can dispense hundreds of solids at small scales while reducing human intervention, making them suitable for comprehensive HTE screening and potentially relevant to drug-discovery workflows. However, the excerpt does not provide quantitative throughput rates such as wells or compounds per hour, formulation-specific performance data, or direct comparisons among commercial platforms. It also gives no purchase, lease, operating, or maintenance costs for Chemspeed FLEX, SWING, Quantos, SWAVE, or other systems. It only states that automated robotic dispensing requires significant capital investment and laboratory space, and may experience downtime from instrument malfunctions.

## pqac-00000036

From text 'nsouli2025advancingorganicchemistry pages 11-11'.

Reem Nsouli, Gaurav Galiyan, and Laura K. G. Ackerman-Biegasiewicz. Advancing organic chemistry using high‐throughput experimentation. Angewandte Chemie International Edition, Sep 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202506588, doi:10.1002/anie.202506588. This article has 46 citations.

The excerpt provides qualitative performance information on automated solid dispensing for high-throughput experimentation, but it does not provide purchase, leasing, operating, or maintenance costs for Chemspeed FLEX, SWING, Quantos, or other commercial systems. Solid dispensing is described as more difficult than liquid handling because powders may be light, fluffy, heavy, electrostatically charged, hygroscopic, or granular, creating measurement errors. Chemspeed SWING and the Mettler Toledo XPR Automatic Balance are characterized as more accurate for dispensing larger masses, but unsuitable for small target quantities. More recent systems—including Chemspeed FLEX, Chemspeed SWILE, Mettler Toledo CHRONECT, and Unchained Labs—can measure low- to sub-milligram quantities. Nevertheless, the systems discussed cannot dispense nanomole-scale solid quantities with acceptable error. AbbVie’s Chembead approach, which coats small glass beads with chemicals, is presented as a solution for sub-milligram and microgram dispensing and as effective across diverse academic and industrial reaction setups. The passage does not give numerical accuracy, dispensing throughput, comparative drug-discovery or formulation data, or self-driving-lab benchmarking. It also does not mention the Chemspeed Quantos platform or provide instrument pricing.

From text 'christensen2022thedevelopmentand pages 62-68'.

Melodie Deniz Christensen. The development and applications of autonomous process optimization systems. Text, Jan 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.14288/1.0422385, doi:10.14288/1.0422385. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides only broad context relevant to automated solid dispensing and Chemspeed systems; it does not report quantitative dispensing accuracy, powder-dose precision, dispensing failure rates, or direct comparisons among Chemspeed FLEX, SWING, Quantos, and other commercial platforms. It identifies Chemspeed Technologies as one of the dominant vendors in high-throughput experimentation (HTE), alongside Unchained Labs and Tecan. The described high-throughput integrated systems combine a solid handler with liquid handling, stirring and temperature control, translocation, and a robotic deck for multiple microplate reactors. Their principal applications are parallel synthesis, reaction optimization, and reaction profiling, which are relevant to drug-discovery workflows. The excerpt states that HTE platforms can reach approximately 96–1536 reactions per day, with 384- and 1536-well workflows generally fully automated at nanomole scale. It also notes the general relationship that increasing throughput is accompanied by miniaturization and reduced material requirements. No purchase prices, operating costs, or quotations for Chemspeed FLEX, SWING, Quantos, or other commercial systems appear in the supplied pages. Therefore, this source can support qualitative claims about Chemspeed’s market position, integrated solid-handling architecture, and drug-discovery throughput, but not the requested accuracy benchmarks, cost analysis, or product-by-product performance comparison.

Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000039

From text 'lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 13-15'.

Adam Lisowski, Henryk Żołnowski, Keyan Villat, Alec Schmidt, Edy Mariano, Jean-Charles Cousty, Jérôme Guérin, Ashley Stark, Frédéric Vasserot, Achim Ammon, David Gueller, Florian de Nanteuil, Jean-Jacques Schwartz, Mathias Cherbuin, Marc Kunze, Giuseppe Tommaso Costanzo, and Pascal Miéville. High-throughput solid microsampling through stochastic robotic automation. Communications Chemistry, Jul 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-026-02153-w, doi:10.1038/s42004-026-02153-w. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt indicates that powder properties affect automated dispensing primarily through sampling feasibility and the width of the dispensed-mass distribution, rather than through the fundamental precision of the weighing process. Precision is mainly controlled by analytical-balance repeatability and accuracy, together with environmental factors such as vibration, airflow fluctuations, and electrostatic disturbances. Particle size and Carr index are specifically discussed: vacuum assistance improves capillary filling, especially for powders with larger particles and higher Carr indices, while passive sampling shows a marked performance threshold at a Carr index of about 30. Below this threshold, sampling success is close to 96% when particle size is smaller than the capillary’s internal diameter; performance decreases for higher-Carr-index powders. The excerpt also notes that sub-milligram accuracy is more vulnerable to fixed balance uncertainty and powder-specific effects, while milligram dispensing is more linear and consistent. Cohesion, hygroscopicity, particle shape, and Hausner ratio are not directly characterized in the supplied passage, although some may be related to flow and compressibility. No information is provided here about containment requirements, occupational exposure bands (OEBs), occupational exposure limits (OELs), or engineering controls for dispensing potent pharmaceutical compounds.


---

## pqac-00000040

From text 'pinzon2012modellingofdosatora pages 62-65'.

OA Angulo Pinzon. Modelling of dosator filling and discharge. Unknown journal, 2012.

The excerpt indicates that powder flow and handling properties strongly influence dosator filling reliability, dose retention, and weight accuracy. Cohesive powders and materials with poor flow—such as many fine APIs—are difficult to handle and may be unsuitable for small-dose filling. In intermittent automated operation, adequate flow is particularly important because the dose must remain in the dosator cavity while being transferred under acceleration; otherwise, loss or variation can reduce the dispensing success rate. Particle size and shape affect blend behavior, while excipient selection and engineering can improve flow, reduce cohesion, adhesion, and friction. The cited lactose example shows that crystalline, hard, brittle particles with good flowability and low moisture content can be advantageous. The passage mentions tapped density measurements used to calculate Hausner ratio and Carr’s index as basic indicators of powder flowability, but the excerpt does not provide their numerical thresholds or directly describe electrostatic charge or hygroscopicity effects. It also does not specify containment requirements, occupational exposure bands (OEB), or occupational exposure limits (OEL) for potent compounds. Those requirements therefore cannot be established from this excerpt and would require separate process-containment and industrial-hygiene guidance.

## pqac-00000041

From text 'hou2024developmentofa pages 64-67'.

Peter Chung-Hsien Hou. Development of a micro-feeder for cohesive pharmaceutical powders. Dissertation, Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.48730/4gp7-jb67, doi:10.48730/4gp7-jb67. This article has 2 citations.

The excerpt indicates that powder cohesion and adhesion can substantially reduce dispensing accuracy and reliability by increasing interparticle resistance, tensile strength, clogging, and flow-rate variability. Moisture and relative humidity promote liquid bridges, surface tension, and negative capillary pressure, increasing cohesiveness and changing bulk density and flowability; water may also lubricate and compact powders or cause particle softening and swelling. Smaller particles have greater specific surface area, which increases van der Waals, electrostatic, and surface-tension forces and generally decreases flowability. Irregular particle shapes increase surface area, cohesive forces, mechanical interlocking, contact area, and friction, whereas more rounded particles can improve flow. Electrostatic charging should be minimized through suitable construction materials because it can interfere with powder movement and contribute to adhesion or blockage. These effects can lead to inconsistent mass flow and lower automated dispensing success unless controlled through fluidization, granulation, coating, environmental control, appropriate surface finish, and prevention of stagnant zones or ratholes. The excerpt does not discuss Hausner ratio or Carr index, although these are commonly used indirect indicators of flowability and could help predict dispensing performance. It also provides no information on potent-compound containment requirements, including occupational exposure bands (OEBs) or occupational exposure limits (OELs).

From text 'pinzon2012modellingofdosator pages 62-65'.

OA Angulo Pinzon. Modelling of dosator filling and discharge. Unknown journal, 2012.

The excerpt provides partial information relevant to automated powder dispensing accuracy and success. Cohesive powders are identified as unsuitable for the dosator process under the stated understanding, and intermittent operation imposes more demanding flow-property requirements so that a dose remains in the cavity during transfer. Poor API flow properties therefore create handling and dosing challenges. Powder characteristics, including particle shape and particle size, affect bulk-powder behaviour; α-lactose monohydrate is described as crystalline, predominantly pyramidal, hard, brittle, and generally flowable, making it a commonly used excipient. Moisture is also relevant: the machines lack environmental control to prevent moisture-content variation, while lactose has low free moisture. Carr index and Hausner ratio are mentioned as flowability measures derived from tapped density, but the excerpt does not explain their quantitative relationship with dispensing accuracy or success rate. The cited passage does not discuss electrostatic charge. It also contains no information about containment requirements, occupational exposure bands (OEB), occupational exposure limits (OEL), or engineering controls for potent compounds. Consequently, those safety and containment aspects cannot be established from this excerpt.

## pqac-00000043

From text 'hou2024developmentofa pages 106-108'.

Peter Chung-Hsien Hou. Development of a micro-feeder for cohesive pharmaceutical powders. Dissertation, Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.48730/4gp7-jb67, doi:10.48730/4gp7-jb67. This article has 2 citations.

The excerpt provides partial information relevant to automated powder dispensing accuracy, primarily concerning powder flow and physical characterization. It identifies cohesive materials, small quantities, and long-term operational accuracy as important challenges in micro-feeder design. Particle size, particle-size distribution, and sphericity were measured using dynamic imaging, indicating that particle morphology is treated as a relevant material property. Bulk, tapped, and true densities were also measured; the excerpt notes that bulk density depends on powder preparation, treatment, storage, and disturbance, while tapped density reflects packing after controlled tapping. These properties support calculation of the Hausner ratio, defined as tapped density divided by bulk density, which is used to interpret powder flowability. Flowability was additionally assessed using a shear-cell tester and the flow function coefficient (ffc), calculated as major principal consolidation stress divided by unconfined yield strength; higher ffc values indicate better flowability. Poor flowability or cohesion would generally be expected to increase feeding variability and reduce dispensing success, but this excerpt does not provide quantitative accuracy or success-rate results. It does not discuss electrostatic charge, hygroscopicity, Carr index effects, or containment requirements such as occupational exposure bands (OEBs), occupational exposure limits (OELs), enclosure performance, or engineering controls for potent compounds.

## pqac-00000044

From text 'ekenlebie2015pharmaceuticalprocessoptimisation pages 69-75'.

EP Ekenlebie. Pharmaceutical process optimisation of bulk lyophilisates: implications of powder handling. Unknown journal, 2015.

The excerpt supports the conclusion that powder flow properties, particularly compressibility, Hausner ratio, Carr index, interparticle friction, and shear behavior, are important determinants of automated dispensing performance. Good-flowing powders are described as less compressible, having low compressibility indices and low particulate friction. Hausner ratio provides an indication of flowability, with ratios of 1.12–1.18 associated with free-flowing powders, while Carr classifies angle-of-repose values of 31–35 as good; however, the excerpt does not directly quantify dispensing accuracy or success rate for particular values. Shear-cell testing can provide more detailed information relevant to hopper and feeder design, including yield strength, internal friction, and tensile strength. Before dispensing, stored powders were sieved to break up agglomerates, and annealed powders were aerated to condition them. Dispensing was conducted under controlled temperature and relative humidity, indicating that environmental conditions can influence powder handling. The excerpt does not provide specific information about cohesion, electrostatic charge, hygroscopicity, particle shape, or their individual effects on dosing accuracy. It also does not state containment requirements or occupational exposure band (OEB) and occupational exposure limit (OEL) values for potent compounds. Glove-box operation, nitrogen purge, and controlled powder transfer are shown for one dispensing setup, but these should not be interpreted as complete OEB/OEL requirements.
