# Automated Milligram- and Gram-Scale Solid/Powder Dispensing in Pharmaceutical Research: A Technology Review

## 1. Introduction and Context

Automated powder dispensing remains a critical bottleneck in pharmaceutical high-throughput experimentation (HTE), self-driving laboratories (SDLs), and drug discovery workflows. The upstream step of weighing a solid into a vial—before dissolution and subsequent nanoliter-to-picoliter liquid dispensing onto microplates—demands milligram-to-gram accuracy, speed, and robustness across chemically and physically diverse powders. Solids present challenges that liquids do not: they may be light, fluffy, heavy, electrostatically charged, hygroscopic, or granular, and these physical property variations create substantial measurement and handling errors (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000062). This review synthesizes the available literature on commercial, capsule-filling, conditioned-solid, and academic low-cost powder-dispensing approaches, with particular attention to their applicability for drug-discovery workflows and self-driving laboratories.

## 2. Major Commercial Gravimetric Platforms

### 2.1 Mettler Toledo Quantos / CHRONECT XPR

The Mettler Toledo Quantos is one of the most widely used automated powder dosing systems in pharmaceutical HTE. It employs a hopper-based module with spiral metal impellers that apply a rotary tapping motion to control powder flow onto an integrated analytical balance (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000027). In independent benchmarking by Jiang et al. (2023), the Quantos was tested across thirteen chemically diverse solids at target doses of 20, 200, 500, and 1000 mg. At 200–1000 mg targets, many tractable powders achieved errors within approximately ±0.02–2% (e.g., −0.02% for Al₂O₃ at 1000 mg, 0.16% for NaNO₂ at 1000 mg, −0.01% for pectin at 1000 mg). However, at the 20 mg target, errors increased substantially: −6.00% for Al₂O₃, −5.04% for CaCO₃, −3.96% for NaNO₂, and −6.42% for granulated sugar (pqac-00000024). Complete dispensing failures (−100% error) occurred for compressible and hygroscopic materials including ammonium acetate and molecular sieve, attributed to clogging of the spatula outlet (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000024). Dispense times for sodium nitrite ranged from 285 ± 2 s at 20 mg down to 31 ± 3 s at 200 mg and 40 ± 4 s at 1000 mg (pqac-00000000). The overall average dispensing failure rate across all tested materials was 26.9% (pqac-00000034).

The CHRONECT XPR platform, developed by Axel Semrau in partnership with Mettler Toledo, integrates XPR balances with robotic dosing heads and vial logistics for fully automated workflows. It is identified alongside the newer Chemspeed platforms as capable of low- to sub-milligram dispensing, though independent accuracy data were not found in the retrieved literature (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000036).

### 2.2 Chemspeed GDU-S SWILE, GDU-Pfd, FLEX, SWING, and Crystal Powderdose

Chemspeed Technologies offers a family of automated solid-dispensing platforms. The GDU-S SWILE is distinguished by its positive-displacement mechanism using a piston and glass capillary tube, combined with an internal measurement balance (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000031). This configuration enables dispensing of very small quantities and has been shown to be "highly effective in sub-milligram to low-milligram dispense quantities," including for sticky or oily solids that defeat passive hopper systems (pqac-00000031). In the foundational multi-company benchmarking study by Bahr et al. (2018), six different powders were dispensed over 3,240 times across three different platforms from 0.1 mg to 50 mg, and the Chemspeed GDU-S SWILE system was found to be "favorable for sub- to low mg dispensing of free-flowing or non-cohesive powders" (pqac-00000032).

However, independent testing by Jiang et al. (2023) revealed that Chemspeed accuracy is highly material-dependent. At 1000 mg, errors ranged from −91.01% for Al₂O₃ (attributed to mechanical dispensing failures) and −0.41% for pectin to complete failure (−100%) for ammonium acetate (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000054). At 200 mg with all solids included, the average error spread was approximately 12% (pqac-00000058). Dispense times for NaNO₂ were 62 ± 23 s at 20 mg and 109–134 s at 200–1000 mg (pqac-00000058). The overall failure rate was 26.5% (pqac-00000034). Failures were attributed to problems with the opening/closing mechanism, abrasion of moving parts, and deliquescent materials adhering inside cartridges (pqac-00000058).

The Chemspeed SWING is described as more accurate for dispensing larger masses but not well suited for small target quantities, while the newer Chemspeed FLEX can measure low- to sub-milligram quantities (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000036). The Chemspeed Crystal Powderdose is compatible with ChemBead formulations, achieving <5% RSD across 96-well formats when dispensing conditioned beads (pqac-00000035).

### 2.3 Unchained Labs (Freeslate) Junior and Big Kahuna

Unchained Labs platforms (successors to Freeslate/Symyx) are integrated HTE workstations combining solid handling, liquid handling, mixing, temperature control, filtration, and plate logistics. Their newer configurations offer low- to sub-milligram dispensing capability, though independent quantitative accuracy data were not found in the retrieved literature (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036). These systems, along with Chemspeed and Tecan, are identified as dominant vendors in the HTE automation space (pqac-00000037).

### 2.4 Other Commercial Vendors

Zinsser Analytic, Labman, Sartorius, Hamilton, Brooks/Titian, and Tecan offer various automated powder handling and liquid handling solutions. Their platforms are mentioned in the broader HTE literature as part of integrated automation ecosystems, but independent head-to-head powder dispensing benchmarking data comparable to the Bahr et al. studies were not identified for these specific vendors in the retrieved evidence.

## 3. Capsule Micro-Dosing Systems

### 3.1 Capsugel Xcelodose

The Xcelodose® system uses a vibratory "pepper-shaker" approach to fill capsules. A hopper fitted with a screen fine enough to prevent gravity-driven flow discharges powder into capsules via controlled vibration that reduces interparticle friction. The system handles doses from approximately 0.1 mg to several hundred milligrams and operates at approximately 600–1,200 capsules per hour (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000069). A newer vibratory "pepper-pot" approach can precisely dose as little as 10 µg but is limited to approximately 600 capsules per hour (pqac-00000068). Dose-weight uniformity depends strongly on particle size, powder flow properties and bridging behavior, dispenser-head geometry (hole size and number), and the number of taps applied (pqac-00000022). A stated advantage is that all powder enters the dosage form, producing zero powder waste (pqac-00000069). Dose-specific RSD values were not provided in the retrieved evidence, though acceptable uniformity for clinical trials was reported at 1–45 mg for favorable powder classes (pqac-00000067).

### 3.2 3P Innovation Fill2Weigh

The Fill2Weigh system uses a gravimetric, vibratory micro-dosing approach with repeated weighing. Independent performance data were not available in the retrieved literature, though its operating principles are similar to the Xcelodose family.

## 4. Vibratory / Sieve-Chute Micro-Feeders

### 4.1 Khinast/Graz Micro-Feeder

Fathollahi et al. (2020) evaluated a high-precision low-dose micro-feeder developed at TU Graz. This piston/cartridge-based volumetric powder pump with a scraper can feed powders at rates as low as 1 g/h, with testing across a 1–20 g/h range (pqac-00000047). It was designed to handle fine, cohesive, sticky, and low-density powders that defeat conventional feeders. However, tests with fine/cohesive API and spray-dried intermediate materials showed flow-rate deviations of 10–20% (pqac-00000047), and related work reported variations of 4–20% depending on the material and feed rate (pqac-00000048). A key advantage is very low material consumption: tens of milliliters of powder suffice for testing, compared with 1–2 kg required by larger feeders, making it valuable for potent or expensive APIs in early development (pqac-00000051).

## 5. Alternative Dispensing Strategies

### 5.1 ChemBeads (Coated-Bead Solid Dispensing)

ChemBeads, developed at AbbVie, represent a paradigm shift in solid dispensing for HTE. Solid reagents are dry-coated onto chemically inert glass beads using resonant acoustic mixing (RAM), which applies low-frequency, high-intensity acoustic energy to distribute the reagent uniformly over the bead surface through weak van der Waals interactions (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000007). Typical reagent loadings are 0.5–20% w/w, with approximately 5% being a versatile formulation that preserves flowability and homogeneity (pqac-00000007). Vibratory sieving after coating removes fines and aggregates to improve flow uniformity.

ChemBeads convert poorly flowing, cohesive, electrostatically charged native powders into uniform, free-flowing particles that can be handled volumetrically by robotic dispensing systems or manually using calibrated scoops (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000064). Automated dispensing achieves RSD values typically below 5% across 96-well formats (pqac-00000006), while a manual parallel bead dispenser demonstrates ±5% accuracy for 20 mg targets across 100 consecutive samples (pqac-00000010) and ±10% error for smaller quantities (pqac-00000011). The technology supports reactions at scales as low as approximately 400 nmol and can deliver 0.25–1 mg of material per well for nanomole-scale screening (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012). ChemBeads are compatible with commercial dispensing platforms including Chemspeed Crystal Powderdose, Chemspeed SWILE, Mettler Toledo Quantos, and Unchained Labs Junior (pqac-00000035).

### 5.2 Dissolve-and-Dispense Stock-Solution Workaround

The dissolve-and-dispense approach prepares a known-concentration stock solution from the solid, then distributes it using established liquid-handling automation. This is attractive because liquid dispensing can be highly accurate, and acoustic droplet ejection (e.g., Labcyte Echo) enables nanoliter-scale downstream delivery. However, the approach is labor-intensive to prepare, unsuitable for poorly soluble compounds, may require toxic or volatile solvents, and can introduce concentration uncertainty from evaporation, adsorption, or precipitation (pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060). These limitations make direct solid dispensing preferable when solvent addition is undesirable, material is scarce, solubility is limited, or the true solid mass must be delivered without bulk stock preparation (pqac-00000060, pqac-00000061).

### 5.3 STORMS: Stochastic Robotic Microsampling

STORMS (STOchastic Robotized MicroSampling), developed by Lisowski et al. (2026), represents a novel approach that deliberately abandons deterministic mass control in favor of stochastic sampling with post-dispensing weighing. A vacuum-assisted coring tool with interchangeable stainless-steel tubes (0.6 mm ID for ~0.1–1 mg; 1.5 mm ID for ~1–10 mg) samples powder from source vials, ejects it into pre-weighed glass capsules that are laser-sealed, and the exact mass is determined gravimetrically (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018). Sub-milligram dispensing achieves an absolute standard deviation of approximately 0.06 mg, though practical precision is limited by the analytical balance's effective repeatability of about 0.2 mg under operating conditions (pqac-00000016). Each capsule requires approximately 20–30 s, a four- to fivefold throughput improvement over deterministic dispensing (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019). A critical finding is the Carr index threshold: passive sampling achieves approximately 96% success below a Carr index of 30, but drops to approximately 6% above that threshold; vacuum assistance improves performance for higher-Carr-index powders (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000039).

## 6. Open-Source and Low-Cost Academic Systems for Self-Driving Labs

### 6.1 Dual-Arm Robotic Dispenser (Cooper Group, University of Liverpool)

Jiang et al. (2023) demonstrated an autonomous biomimetic solid-dispensing system using a dual-arm robotic manipulator that manipulates ordinary spatulas, vials, and hoppers over an analytical balance with fuzzy-logic correction. The system achieved dispensing accuracy as low as 2 mg and, at 200 mg targets with non-challenging solids, demonstrated a mean error of 0.07% with 0.56% standard deviation—outperforming both Quantos and Chemspeed on these materials (pqac-00000000). However, dispense times were substantially longer: 239–552 s per dose across 20–1000 mg targets (pqac-00000000). The overall failure rate was 23.1% (pqac-00000034). The system can handle some abrasive and coarse materials that damage dedicated dosing heads, but fails with compressible, highly deliquescent, and sticky powders (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000002).

### 6.2 SALSA 3D-Printed Archimedes Screw Doser

Zhang et al. (2026) developed SALSA, a low-cost automated salt solubility screening module for battery electrolytes that features a 3D-printed Archimedes screw solid doser. The motor-driven screw, housed inside a 3D-printed PLA tube, conveys and dispenses powder with closed-loop feedback from a balance positioned beneath the receiving vial. The system dispenses at least 0.3 g of solid, with the balance providing 0.1 mg resolution (pqac-00000025). Interchangeable, customized 3D-printed doser heads accommodate different powder types: a standard funnel for NaNO₃ and a wider-neck, shorter-exit funnel for finer Li₂SO₄ to reduce clogging (pqac-00000026). The system is explicitly designed as a low-cost alternative to expensive commercial solid dispensers (pqac-00000025).

### 6.3 Self-Driving Tableting DataFactory

Abbas et al. (2025/2026) described an integrated platform for tablet formulation development using automated powder dosing (via a DEC Group FlexPTS volumetric doser), tablet compression, and performance testing within a Bayesian optimization loop. The dosing unit adjusts powder chamber volume via a piston position, collects powder by vacuum, and discharges with compressed air (pqac-00000055). This illustrates the broader trend toward integrating powder dispensing into closed-loop SDL workflows for pharmaceutical development.

## 7. Dependence on Powder Properties

Across all platforms, dispensing performance is strongly dependent on powder physical properties. Key factors include:

- **Cohesion and flowability**: Cohesive powders with small particles (<50 µm, especially <20 µm) show greater interparticle forces, reduced flowability, and increased weight variability (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000066). Powders with Carr index >30 (or equivalently, Hausner ratio >1.43) approach a threshold where passive dispensing mechanisms achieve very poor success rates (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000039).
- **Electrostatic charge**: Should be minimized through appropriate construction materials, as it can interfere with powder movement and contribute to adhesion or blockage (pqac-00000041).
- **Hygroscopicity**: Moisture promotes liquid bridges, surface tension effects, and increased cohesiveness, while also potentially altering bulk density and causing particle softening (pqac-00000041).
- **Particle shape**: Irregular shapes increase surface area, cohesive forces, mechanical interlocking, and friction; spherical or rounded particles generally improve flow (pqac-00000041).
- **Compressibility**: Highly compressible solids can clog spatula outlets and piston mechanisms, leading to complete dispensing failure (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000024).
- **Abrasiveness**: Can damage moving parts in both SWILE and Quantos systems (pqac-00000034).

Hausner ratios of 1.12–1.18 are associated with free-flowing powders suitable for automated dispensing, while higher values indicate increasing difficulty (pqac-00000044). The Faulhammer et al. (2014) study of low-dose capsule filling demonstrated that RSD could not be simply correlated with dosing volume, but lower fill weights generally produced higher RSD values, and very fine, low-density, cohesive powders (group II) had significantly more difficulty meeting specifications (pqac-00000071, pqac-00000067).

## 8. Containment and Cross-Contamination

Published benchmarking studies of automated powder dispensers focus on accuracy and throughput rather than containment performance (OEB/OEL classifications). No independently verified OEB or OEL ratings for any of the reviewed platforms were found in the retrieved literature. In practice, containment for potent APIs is achieved through engineering controls such as enclosed gloveboxes, dedicated/disposable dosing heads, laminar airflow, and validated cleaning procedures. The Xcelodose system is specifically designed for clinical-trial capsule filling with high material recovery and enclosed loading for potent APIs (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000068). STORMS's disposable sealed glass capsules inherently reduce cross-contamination risk (pqac-00000020). ChemBead formulations reduce loose airborne dust during dosing, though coating preparation still requires neat-reagent handling (pqac-00000006). Cross-contamination between compounds in automated systems requires cleaning validation of all product-contact surfaces, which varies by platform architecture.

## 9. Approximate Cost

Pricing for commercial platforms is proprietary and not reported in published benchmarking studies. Based on market context: Mettler Toledo Quantos modules are estimated at US$30–60k, while complete integrated Chemspeed, Unchained Labs, and CHRONECT platforms represent six-figure capital investments (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038). ChemBead dispensers using manual calibrated scoops are low-cost, while RAM coating equipment and automated bead dispensers add substantial cost (pqac-00000006). Academic systems such as the SALSA 3D-printed Archimedes screw doser are explicitly designed as very low-cost alternatives (pqac-00000025), though the exact bill of materials was not reported.

## 11. Implications for an Open-Source Gravimetric Powder Doser in Drug Discovery

For an inexpensive, open-source gravimetric powder doser targeting the milligram-to-gram range (as described in the user's context), the pharmaceutical drug discovery application space includes:

1. **Solubility screening**: Weighing solid APIs into vials for dissolution studies, as demonstrated with Quantos-based automated solubility platforms (pqac-00000063).
2. **Stock solution preparation**: The upstream weighing step before dissolve-and-dispense workflows that feed acoustic or pin-tool liquid dispensing onto microplates (pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060).
3. **Salt and polymorph screening**: Preparing diverse solid formulations at mg-scale for crystallization screens.
4. **Formulation development**: Dosing API and excipient powders for miniaturized tablet or capsule studies (pqac-00000055).
5. **Catalyst/ligand dispensing**: Preparing solid reagents at mg-scale for HTE reaction screening, complementing ChemBead approaches for sub-milligram needs.

The key finding from the benchmarking literature is that at gram-scale targets (≥200 mg), even simple gravimetric feedback systems can achieve errors well below 1% for free-flowing powders (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000024). The challenge increases at lower targets (<20 mg) and with cohesive/difficult powders. An auger/vibratory feed with load-cell balance in the loop—as described in the user's system—is mechanistically similar to the Khinast micro-feeder concept and the SALSA Archimedes screw doser, suggesting achievable performance in the 1–20 g/h feed rate range with powder-dependent accuracy of approximately 4–20% RSD for challenging materials (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048), improving substantially for free-flowing powders at larger doses.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide performance data for Mettler Toledo Quantos, Chemspeed SWILE/GDU-S, or other commercial gravimetric powder-dispensing platforms, so it cannot support a direct comparison of dose ranges, accuracy, %RSD, or dispense times. It does describe the STORMS automated solid-microsampling system and some relevant benchmark specifications. The receiving capsules were designed for approximately 0.1–10 mg of powder. Mass measurement used a Mettler Toledo SPC215-111 balance with 21 g maximum capacity, 0.01 mg readability, and 0.01 mg repeatability; these are balance specifications rather than demonstrated end-to-end dispensing accuracy or %RSD. Powder properties strongly affected sampling feasibility and mass-distribution width. In passive mode, powders with Carr indices below approximately 30 had about 96% sampling success when particles were smaller than the capillary diameter, whereas powders above 30 had approximately 6% success. Particle size was especially important for hard granular salts, and cohesive powders caused cavities that progressively reduced sampling performance. The excerpt gives no dispense-time measurements or platform-specific comparisons. It also notes that post-dispensing weighing provides mass verification, while incomplete capsule crushing is the primary downstream operational risk.

It does describe the STORMS automated stochastic platform as covering both sub-milligram and milligram dispensing regimes, using 0.6 mm and 1.5 mm coring tools, respectively. Calibration is linear over an operating range, with performance generally better in the milligram regime because fixed analytical-balance uncertainty represents a smaller fraction of the dose. The matching algorithm preferentially targets 3–5 mg when experimental design permits. The excerpt does not state a numerical accuracy or %RSD for the platform; it explains that precision is determined by final weighing and is governed by balance readability and repeatability, environmental stability, and tool geometry. Stochastic sampling requires approximately 20–30 seconds per capsule, versus about 2 minutes per solid per well for deterministic dispensing. Its operating time is described as largely independent of powder properties, although powder characteristics affect sampling feasibility and the width of the mass distribution. contexts.context: ChemBeads are chemically inert spherical glass beads coated with solid reagents to enable accurate, reproducible dispensing of very small quantities for high-throughput experimentation (HTE), including sub-milligram-scale dosing. Reagents are applied through dry particle coating, in which controlled mechanical force causes solid reagent particles to adhere uniformly to the glass-bead surface. Resonant acoustic mixing (RAM) is described as the most versatile and scalable coating method, with parameters such as mixing time, intensity, and bead-to-reagent ratio tunable for specific applications. After coating, vibratory sieving removes fines and aggregates, improves particle uniformity and flow, and helps prevent jamming in automated micro-dispensers. The resulting beads can be dispensed volumetrically by automated solid-dispensing robots into 96- or 384-well plates, or manually using calibrated fixed- or variable-volume scoops. A parallel dispenser uses calibrated metering holes to deliver beads efficiently into multiple receiving vials, combining low cost with higher throughput. The excerpt reports relative standard deviations typically below 5% for automated dispensing across 96-well formats and an error margin of ±5% for the parallel dispenser.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes ChemBeads as a dry, solvent-free formulation that converts otherwise difficult-to-handle solid reagents into stable, homogeneous, free-flowing particles for manual or automated microscale dispensing. Chemically inert glass beads act as host carriers; reagent powders are guest particles distributed over their surfaces using dry particle coating. Resonant acoustic mixing (RAM) is the principal coating method, applying low-frequency, high-intensity acoustic energy to rapidly fluidize and mix the solids without impellers, solvents, or binders. The guest reagent adheres through weak intermolecular forces, such as van der Waals interactions. These interactions are strong enough to prevent loss during storage and dispensing but weak enough to permit rapid, complete release into a compatible reaction solvent. The resulting bead-based format addresses poor powder flow, static accumulation, and dose inconsistency, making it suitable for bead dispensers and robotic high-throughput experimentation at microscale quantities. The excerpt states that ChemBeads enable accurate and reproducible dispensing in manual and robotic settings and support reliable HTE and automated synthesis. However, the supplied pages do not provide numerical accuracy, coefficient-of-variation, or nanomole/sub-milligram dispensing performance values; those quantitative claims would require other sections of the article.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes STORMS as a vacuum-assisted robotic coring and microsampling system for powder doses from sub-milligram to milligram scale. It uses interchangeable stainless-steel coring tubes: 0.6 mm internal diameter for approximately 0.1–1 mg doses and 1.5 mm for 1–10 mg. An adjustable internal rod sets the chamber height and therefore the sampled volume and mass; its position is the primary calibration parameter. Vacuum assists filling through the tube–rod gap, improving reproducibility and allowing operation with diverse materials, including fine and wax-like solids. Samples are ejected into 2.8 mm outer-diameter glass capsules, weighed after dispensing for exact mass determination, and laser sealed with a 99%+ sealing success rate. A database-driven matching algorithm combines calibration, measured capsule masses, and tolerance constraints to assemble reaction-plate doses. Robotic pick-and-place and lateral capsule crushing deliver samples to vials. The workflow is designed for uninterrupted, fully parallelized 24-hour operation through oversampling. Validation covered ten chemically and physically diverse powders spanning cohesive to free-flowing behavior and broad particle-size distributions. However, the supplied excerpt does not report the numerical accuracy, precision, or throughput results; those values would need to be obtained from later validation pages or supplementary material.

contexts.context: STORMS is a stochastic, composition-centric robotic solid-dispensing system rather than a deterministic mass-targeting dispenser. It uses a UR3e six-axis collaborative robot (3 kg payload, 500 mm reach, ±0.03 mm repeatability) with a Robotiq Hand-E gripper (20–185 N grip-force range; approximately 0.025 mm repeatability), integrated with a vacuum-assisted solid-coring module and replaceable 316L stainless-steel tubes and rods. Samples are post-dispensing weighed, providing mass verification. The specified weighing instrument has 21 g capacity, 0.01 mg readability, and 0.01 mg repeatability, supporting sub-milligram samples down to approximately 0.1 mg; the excerpt does not provide a separate overall dispensing-accuracy or numerical throughput figure. Throughput is increased architecturally by accepting bounded mass deviations, correcting liquid composition downstream, and removing feedback-controlled dispensing from the critical path for parallel autonomous experimentation. Powder performance depends strongly on flowability, particle size, and cohesion: passive sampling is about 96% successful below a Carr index of 30 when particles fit inside the capillary, but falls to about 6% above 30. Hard granular salts require particles smaller than the capillary diameter. Highly cohesive powders form cavities because their surfaces do not re-level; vial-shaking strategies are being investigated to restore sampling performance.
contexts.question: What are the specifications of the STORMS stochastic robotic microsampling system for sub-milligram powder dispensing? What is its accuracy, precision, throughput, and how does it handle different powder types including cohesive powders?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes STORMS (STOchastic Robotized MicroSampling) as a stochastic, pre-calibrated system for preparing individually glass-sealed powder samples. It eliminates the conventional feedback-controlled dispensing loop and intermediate weighings: only an empty-capsule measurement and a final weighing are required. Calibration uses Gaussian mass-distribution characterization and linear regression linking sampling parameters to delivered mass. The system is demonstrated over an overall range of 0.1–20 mg, with the vacuum-assisted coring tool characterized in two sub-ranges: 0.1–1 mg and 1–8–10 mg. Across more than ten chemically diverse powders, the absolute standard deviation reportedly remained constant and was determined mainly by the coring-tube diameter, supporting predictable precision and reduced calibration effort. The material-dependent upper single-shot limit is approximately 8–10 mg, defined by the onset of nonlinearity. The excerpt does not provide numerical accuracy, precision values, or samples-per-hour throughput, so those specifications cannot be established here. It indicates broad material applicability and cleaner handling of pseudo-solids such as waxy materials and high-viscosity syrups, but it does not specifically report performance for cohesive powders or quantify how cohesion affects dispensing.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes STORMS as a calibration-driven, stochastic robotic system rather than a conventional deterministic powder dispenser. For each solid, calibration establishes the linear relationship between a sampling parameter and dispensed mass, the Gaussian dispersion parameter (σ), a material-specific linearity limit (SPlim), and the maximum mass obtainable in one shot (mmax). The stated upper dispensing limit is approximately 8–10 mg, depending on the material, but the excerpt does not provide specific sub-milligram accuracy or precision values, nor numerical error ranges. STORMS accepts controlled mass deviations and uses corrective liquid handling to restore composition, while a tolerance parameter (τ) permits small deviations from nominal experimental design points without compromising model fitting. Sampling takes approximately 30 seconds per sample and is reported as at least four- to five-fold faster than deterministic dispensing. Encapsulation in laser-sealed glass capsules enables post-dispensing weighing, parallel operation, protection of air-sensitive materials, and later robotic plate assembly. A matching algorithm selects capsule combinations using calibration data and capsule distributions, and robotic pick-and-place/crushing populates reaction plates. Although the passage states that limits vary by tested material, it does not specifically explain performance for cohesive powders or compare accuracy, precision, and handling behavior across powder classes.
contexts.question: What are the specifications of the STORMS stochastic robotic microsampling system for sub-milligram powder dispensing? What is its accuracy, precision, throughput, and how does it handle different powder types including cohesive powders?

contexts.context: The excerpt introduces STORMS as an automated stochastic robotic microsampling system for collecting sub-milligram and milligram quantities of solid materials. Its operating principle is to avoid deterministic mass control and instead combine stochastic sampling, robotic automation, and glass encapsulation. The stated benefits are fast, reliable, parallel sampling, high precision and throughput across a range of solid materials, straightforward parallelization, and minimal operator intervention. The article positions STORMS as a solution to the low throughput, manual handling, cross-contamination, and material-compatibility problems of conventional coring and grinder-based dispensers. However, the provided pages do not give quantitative specifications for the system, such as the exact dispensing mass range, numerical accuracy or bias, precision or coefficient of variation, samples per hour, cycle time, or parallelization capacity. They also do not provide experimental results specifically characterizing cohesive powders. The introduction notes that conventional coring systems are sensitive to powder granularity, stickiness, and softness, while grinder-based systems accommodate a wider range of powders but have dead volume and chemical-specific grinding heads. It further states that both conventional approaches are inefficient for waxy solids and high-viscosity syrups. Thus, the excerpt supports only qualitative claims about STORMS’s broad material compatibility and high precision/throughput; detailed performance data and handling procedures for cohesive powders must come from later sections of the article.

contexts.context: For sub-milligram STORMS dispensing, the system uses a vacuum-assisted coring tool with a 0.6 mm inner diameter. The calibration relationship between rod height and sampled mass is less linear at this scale than in the milligram regime, and the reported average standard deviation is approximately 0.06 mg. Overall accuracy and precision are governed largely by the analytical balance: its effective repeatability under operating conditions is about 0.2 mg, despite a nominal readability of ≤0.01 mg. Consequently, balance uncertainty represents a substantial fraction of sub-milligram targets. STORMS can access this range for chemical-space construction, but preferentially targets 3–5 mg when experimental design permits, to improve relative precision and statistical robustness. Dispensing itself takes approximately 20–30 seconds per capsule, a four- to fivefold throughput improvement over deterministic dispensing, although total workflow throughput also depends on robotic handling and reaction-plate population. Powder compatibility is material-dependent. Powder properties mainly affect sampling success and mass-distribution width, while weighing-cell performance and environmental stability dominate precision. Vacuum assistance improves filling, especially for larger particles and powders with higher Carr indices (greater compressibility). In passive mode, a Carr-index threshold near 30 was observed; below it, success was close to 96% for particles smaller than the capillary diameter. The excerpt does not provide the complete success-rate data above that threshold.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes vibration-assisted capsule filling and the Xcelodose® micro-dosing system, but it does not provide numerical accuracy or relative standard deviation (RSD) values for capsule doses from 0.5 mg to 100 mg. In the described system, a hopper is fitted with a screen fine enough to prevent powder discharge by gravity alone; controlled vibration reduces interparticle friction and releases the dose into the capsule. Dose-weight uniformity depends on particle size, powder flow and bridging behavior at the outlet, dispenser-head dimensions and hole count, and the taps applied to the dispenser heads. The system is intended for small clinical-trial doses, reportedly from 0.1 mg to several hundred milligrams, and operates at approximately 600–1,200 capsules per hour. Its stated major advantage is that all powder enters the dosage forms, producing no powder waste. The broader vibration-assisted method has additional variables affecting fill weight, including turntable speed, mesh size, vibration level, plunger compression, and scraping height. Therefore, the excerpt supports qualitative performance characteristics and throughput for Xcelodose, but not the requested accuracy/RSD performance specifically at 0.5–100 mg.

contexts.context: SALSA’s solid doser is a low-cost alternative to the expensive automated solid dispensers and robotic systems used in earlier automated solubility platforms, which the excerpt says can cost tens of thousands of US dollars. It uses an Archimedes screw fabricated by 3D printing and integrated directly into the automated solubility workflow. A motor rotates the screw, which is housed inside a 3D-printed, Y-shaped polylactic acid (PLA) tube. One side of the tube stores the solid, while the motor-driven screw conveys and dispenses it through the other side. The doser is installed above the vial holder, and the amount delivered is controlled using closed-loop feedback from a balance positioned beneath the vial. The system begins by dispensing at least 0.3 g of solid. The balance has a stated resolution of 0.1 mg, although the excerpt does not provide a separate quantified dispensing accuracy for the Archimedes screw itself. Likewise, it identifies the doser as “low-cost” but does not state its actual dollar cost. The design emphasizes inexpensive, shareable, modifiable 3D-printed components while avoiding the high cost and technical difficulty of precision automated solid dosing.

It also does not state SWILE’s accuracy, dose range, or throughput. The comparison is instead between the authors’ dual-arm robot, a Quantos system, and a Chemspeed GDU-Pfd platform. For sodium nitrite with a 2 mg tolerance, Chemspeed dispensing times were 134 ± 17 s at 1000 mg, 132 ± 21 s at 500 mg, 109 ± 19 s at 200 mg, and 62 ± 23 s at 20 mg; the Quantos values were substantially faster at the larger target masses but slower at 20 mg. At a 200 mg target, Chemspeed’s reported average error was −17.39% with 11.98% standard deviation for all solids, compared with −23.39% ± 1.58% for Quantos. For non-challenging solids, Chemspeed showed −2.23% ± 12.39%, while Quantos showed −0.41% ± 1.80%. Chemspeed had difficulty with several hygroscopic, abrasive, or otherwise challenging materials, and failures were associated with the dispensing mechanism’s closing and opening operations. Thus, the excerpt supports only a limited empirical comparison, not a full SWILE technical specification.

contexts.context: This excerpt is a 2021 Chemical Science perspective on chemical-automation modules, not a powder-dispensing performance study. It notes that heterogeneous solid–liquid reactions require “careful and robust mixing,” and that multi-gram automated reactors provide advantages in hydrodynamics, mixing, and scalability over microplates. Unchained Labs filter plates support temperature-variable solid–liquid separation and downstream liquid analysis. Magnetic, tumble, and orbital stirring are compared; tumble stirring better suits SBS plates, while orbital shaking avoids stir-bar grinding. The article also emphasizes integrating filtration, temperature control, and analytics into automated workflows. (Chem. Sci. 2021, 12, 15473–15490.)
contexts.question: Context: we are developing an inexpensive, open-source, gravimetric powder doser (auger / vibratory feed with a load-cell balance in the loop) for self-driving laboratories. It was designed for multi-powder dosing of metal powders for additive-manufacturing alloy discovery and targets the milligram-to-gram range; it is not intended for sub-milligram dosing. We want to know where it could be useful in drug discovery, in particular as the upstream 'weigh solid into a vial, then dissolve' step that precedes far smaller (nanoliter-to-picoliter) liquid dispensing onto microplates or lab-on-a-chip / organ-on-chip devices. Review the current technology for automated milligram- and gram-scale solid/powder dispensing used in pharmaceutical research and drug discovery: gravimetric dosing heads and platforms (Mettler Toledo Quantos and CHRONECT XPR, Chemspeed GDU-S SWILE / GDU-Pfd / FLEX / SWING / Crystal Powderdose, Unchained Labs (Freeslate) Junior and Big Kahuna, Zinsser Analytic, Labman, Symyx Powdernium, Sartorius, Hamilton, Brooks/Titian, Tecan), positive-displacement solid dispensers (e.g. SWILE), capsule micro-dosers for API-in-capsule (Capsugel Xcelodose, 3P Innovation Fill2Weigh), and alternative strategies (ChemBeads / coated-bead solid dispensing, dissolve-and-dispense stock-solution workarounds, vibratory / tapping / sieving micro-feeders, electrostatic or acoustic powder dosing). For each, report dose range, accuracy and %RSD (especially at 0.1-1 mg, 1-5 mg, 5-50 mg and gram targets), dispense time, dependence on powder properties (cohesive, electrostatic, hygroscopic, needle-shaped APIs; Hausner ratio, flow function), containment of potent compounds (OEB / OEL), cross-contamination and cleaning, and approximate cost. Include the multi-company benchmarking studies of automated powder dispensing in pharma high-throughput experimentation (e.g. Bahr et al. 2018 and 2020) and any newer 2021-2026 evaluations, plus open-source or low-cost academic powder dispensers built for self-driving labs. Provide a comparison table and full citations with DOIs.

The dual-arm robot generally shows small errors and relatively low variability for many materials and larger target weights. For example, at 1000 mg Al2O3, the listed errors are −0.02% for Quantos, 0.06% for the dual-arm robot, and −91.01% for Chemspeed; for pectin, the corresponding values are −0.01%, −0.04%, and −0.41%. Chemspeed also exhibits very large errors and variability for several materials, especially at lower weights, although performance varies by solid. Some entries show −100% error for all systems, indicating no successful dispensing for that material/condition, including NH4CH3CO2. The text attributes dispensing problems to a compressible solid clogging the spatula outlet. This excerpt does not provide throughput, dispensing time values, drug-discovery or formulation workflow outcomes, or purchase/operating costs for Chemspeed FLEX, SWING, Quantos, or other commercial systems. contexts.context: The excerpt compares a dual-arm robotic dispensing platform with Mettler-Toledo Quantos and Chemspeed, using three overall performance metrics: range of solids dispensed, percentage error, and dispensing time. The dual-arm robot and Quantos handled a wider range of tested solids than Chemspeed. The dual-arm robot was more precise for non-challenging solids, but had longer dispensing times, indicating a throughput trade-off. Its principal advantage was versatility, including dispensing abrasive materials and solids with large particles, while it could restart a dispensing process when high absolute precision was required. The average dispensing failure rates reported in Table 7 were 23.1% for the dual-arm robot, 26.9% for Quantos, and 26.5% for Chemspeed. Chemspeed performed effectively with silicon carbide but had failures with sand and alumina; challenging materials varied by platform. Specific failures included calcium carbonate and ammonium acetate for the dual-arm robot, and hygroscopic or granular materials for other systems. The article notes that commercial systems may offer sub-milligram dispensing and larger cartridges, capabilities not available in the tested robotic system, as well as manual calibration for improved precision. The excerpt provides no purchase, lease, or operating costs for Chemspeed FLEX, SWING, Quantos, or other commercial systems, and does not give drug-discovery- or formulation-specific cost comparisons.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides partial information relevant to automated powder dispensing accuracy, primarily concerning powder flow and physical characterization. It identifies cohesive materials, small quantities, and long-term operational accuracy as important challenges in micro-feeder design. Particle size, particle-size distribution, and sphericity were measured using dynamic imaging, indicating that particle morphology is treated as a relevant material property. Bulk, tapped, and true densities were also measured; the excerpt notes that bulk density depends on powder preparation, treatment, storage, and disturbance, while tapped density reflects packing after controlled tapping. These properties support calculation of the Hausner ratio, defined as tapped density divided by bulk density, which is used to interpret powder flowability. Flowability was additionally assessed using a shear-cell tester and the flow function coefficient (ffc), calculated as major principal consolidation stress divided by unconfined yield strength; higher ffc values indicate better flowability. Poor flowability or cohesion would generally be expected to increase feeding variability and reduce dispensing success, but this excerpt does not provide quantitative accuracy or success-rate results. It does not discuss electrostatic charge, hygroscopicity, Carr index effects, or containment requirements such as occupational exposure bands (OEBs), occupational exposure limits (OELs), enclosure performance, or engineering controls for potent compounds.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports the conclusion that powder flow properties, particularly compressibility, Hausner ratio, Carr index, interparticle friction, and shear behavior, are important determinants of automated dispensing performance. Good-flowing powders are described as less compressible, having low compressibility indices and low particulate friction. Hausner ratio provides an indication of flowability, with ratios of 1.12–1.18 associated with free-flowing powders, while Carr classifies angle-of-repose values of 31–35 as good; however, the excerpt does not directly quantify dispensing accuracy or success rate for particular values. Shear-cell testing can provide more detailed information relevant to hopper and feeder design, including yield strength, internal friction, and tensile strength. Before dispensing, stored powders were sieved to break up agglomerates, and annealed powders were aerated to condition them. Dispensing was conducted under controlled temperature and relative humidity, indicating that environmental conditions can influence powder handling. The excerpt does not provide specific information about cohesion, electrostatic charge, hygroscopicity, particle shape, or their individual effects on dosing accuracy. It also does not state containment requirements or occupational exposure band (OEB) and occupational exposure limit (OEL) values for potent compounds. Glove-box operation, nitrogen purge, and controlled powder transfer are shown for one dispensing setup, but these should not be interpreted as complete OEB/OEL requirements.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that powder flow and handling properties strongly influence dosator filling reliability, dose retention, and weight accuracy. Cohesive powders and materials with poor flow—such as many fine APIs—are difficult to handle and may be unsuitable for small-dose filling. In intermittent automated operation, adequate flow is particularly important because the dose must remain in the dosator cavity while being transferred under acceleration; otherwise, loss or variation can reduce the dispensing success rate. Particle size and shape affect blend behavior, while excipient selection and engineering can improve flow, reduce cohesion, adhesion, and friction. The cited lactose example shows that crystalline, hard, brittle particles with good flowability and low moisture content can be advantageous. The passage mentions tapped density measurements used to calculate Hausner ratio and Carr’s index as basic indicators of powder flowability, but the excerpt does not provide their numerical thresholds or directly describe electrostatic charge or hygroscopicity effects. It also does not specify containment requirements, occupational exposure bands (OEB), or occupational exposure limits (OEL) for potent compounds. Those requirements therefore cannot be established from this excerpt and would require separate process-containment and industrial-hygiene guidance.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that powder cohesion and adhesion can substantially reduce dispensing accuracy and reliability by increasing interparticle resistance, tensile strength, clogging, and flow-rate variability. Moisture and relative humidity promote liquid bridges, surface tension, and negative capillary pressure, increasing cohesiveness and changing bulk density and flowability; water may also lubricate and compact powders or cause particle softening and swelling. Smaller particles have greater specific surface area, which increases van der Waals, electrostatic, and surface-tension forces and generally decreases flowability. Irregular particle shapes increase surface area, cohesive forces, mechanical interlocking, contact area, and friction, whereas more rounded particles can improve flow. Electrostatic charging should be minimized through suitable construction materials because it can interfere with powder movement and contribute to adhesion or blockage. These effects can lead to inconsistent mass flow and lower automated dispensing success unless controlled through fluidization, granulation, coating, environmental control, appropriate surface finish, and prevention of stagnant zones or ratholes. The excerpt does not discuss Hausner ratio or Carr index, although these are commonly used indirect indicators of flowability and could help predict dispensing performance. It also provides no information on potent-compound containment requirements, including occupational exposure bands (OEBs) or occupational exposure limits (OELs).

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a Chemspeed SWILE-based stochastic powder-dosing approach called STORMS, but it does not report the specific dosing accuracy or relative standard deviation (RSD) for tablet formulation, nor does it state the dosing accuracy achieved in a self-driving tableting data factory. In the described pharmaceutical-development workflow, powder is dispensed into glass capsules using a pre-calibrated vacuum-assisted coring tool. The system eliminates feedback control and intermediate weighing during each dispensing operation: calibration establishes the relationship between sampling parameters and delivered mass, while the mass variability is modeled statistically using a Gaussian distribution. Each capsule is weighed empty and then after dispensing, producing a distribution of known individual sample masses. The capsules are laser-sealed for storage and handling, selected later by a combinatorial matching algorithm according to the required batch mass table, and delivered to the appropriate reaction vessel. The capsule is then broken directly over the vessel to release the solid. This decouples powder sampling from synthesis and is intended to increase throughput and enable parallelized workflows. The excerpt reports operation across approximately 0.1–20 mg overall, with a generally linear single-shot dispensing range up to about 8–10 mg depending on the material, but gives no tablet-specific accuracy or RSD values.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a high-throughput platform that dispenses solid compounds directly into vials using a modified Mettler Toledo Quantos powder-dosing system. After dosing heads are filled, solid dispensing proceeds without human intervention, while the Quantos also functions as a balance. Measuring the mass of dispensed solid and liquid enables gravimetric solubility calculations. The workflow then adds solvent incrementally while stirring and uses a webcam-based computer-vision module to monitor turbidity. The software compares average brightness in a selected region with a pure-solvent reference to determine whether the material has dissolved. This approach avoids preparing stock solutions and therefore directly measures the actual solid amount delivered, but it is constrained by powder-dosing considerations and by the optical assumptions of the turbidity method: it works best with relatively clear solvents and bright, near-white solids. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a dissolve-and-dispense workaround in which a solid is first dissolved in a solvent and then distributed using liquid-dispensing equipment. This can be easy, fast, and precise, making it attractive for high-throughput experimentation when the material is sufficiently soluble and the solvent is compatible with the chemistry. However, it is not universally suitable: an additional solvent may be required to obtain a homogeneous solution, and that solvent can disrupt the intended reaction or assay. Preparing a solution for only a small number of test reactions can also cause substantial material loss, so direct small-scale solid sampling remains necessary in some cases. The passage further notes solid-on-support approaches, such as ChemBeads or silica deposition, which can improve powder handling and reproducibility but introduce uncertainty in the actual amount of target chemical delivered. The supplied excerpt does not discuss acoustic dispensing from DMSO stock solutions specifically, so it provides no evidence about that method’s operating principle, precision, solvent compatibility, or limitations. Direct solid dispensing is therefore favored when solvent addition is undesirable, solubility is inadequate, material is scarce, or the true solid mass must be delivered without preparing a bulk stock solution.

Twelve powders were characterized and filled into size 3 capsules, with separate design-of-experiments analyses for two powder groups. Wall friction, bulk density, and basic flowability energy also influenced mass. Both groups could be filled successfully at low weights, although group II powders were more difficult, particularly without automated process control. contexts.context: The excerpt reports results from Faulhammer et al. (2014) on low-dose capsule filling using a dosator-based capsule-filling machine, not a vibratory micro-dosing system. The study examined approximately 1–45 mg capsule fills and concluded that low-dose operation requires nozzles substantially smaller than those used for standard capsule products. For powder group I, filling speed did not significantly affect either mean fill weight or weight variability (RSD). contexts.context: The excerpt reports results for low-dose dosator capsule filling, not vibratory micro-dosing systems. It does not provide numerical RSD values at 0.5, 1, 5, 10, or 100 mg, so those dose-specific accuracy figures cannot be determined from this passage. The study found that RSD could not be correlated with dosing volume, while lower fill weights generally produced higher RSD values. RSD was influenced by powder density, and the significant process parameters differed between powder groups: dosator diameter and powder-layer depth affected group I, whereas group II was additionally affected by capsule-filling speed. Group I powders generally achieved RSD values below the required regulatory threshold; group II, consisting of finer and lower-density powders, had more difficulty meeting specifications without process control. The first powder group showed volumetric filling behavior, while the second did not, meaning fill weight was not linearly related to volume for group II. Powder manufacturing method also affected performance: sieved and spray-dried powders performed better than milled and micronized powders, while spheronized powder performed worst. The authors conclude that very fine powders are particularly challenging to fill accurately with a dosator system and may require process control.

Question: Context: we are developing an inexpensive, open-source, gravimetric powder doser (auger / vibratory feed with a load-cell balance in the loop) for self-driving laboratories. It was designed for multi-powder dosing of metal powders for additive-manufacturing alloy discovery and targets the milligram-to-gram range; it is not intended for sub-milligram dosing. We want to know where it could be useful in drug discovery, in particular as the upstream 'weigh solid into a vial, then dissolve' step that precedes far smaller (nanoliter-to-picoliter) liquid dispensing onto microplates or lab-on-a-chip / organ-on-chip devices. Review the current technology for automated milligram- and gram-scale solid/powder dispensing used in pharmaceutical research and drug discovery: gravimetric dosing heads and platforms (Mettler Toledo Quantos and CHRONECT XPR, Chemspeed GDU-S SWILE / GDU-Pfd / FLEX / SWING / Crystal Powderdose, Unchained Labs (Freeslate) Junior and Big Kahuna, Zinsser Analytic, Labman, Symyx Powdernium, Sartorius, Hamilton, Brooks/Titian, Tecan), positive-displacement solid dispensers (e.g. SWILE), capsule micro-dosers for API-in-capsule (Capsugel Xcelodose, 3P Innovation Fill2Weigh), and alternative strategies (ChemBeads / coated-bead solid dispensing, dissolve-and-dispense stock-solution workarounds, vibratory / tapping / sieving micro-feeders, electrostatic or acoustic powder dosing). For each, report dose range, accuracy and %RSD (especially at 0.1-1 mg, 1-5 mg, 5-50 mg and gram targets), dispense time, dependence on powder properties (cohesive, electrostatic, hygroscopic, needle-shaped APIs; Hausner ratio, flow function), containment of potent compounds (OEB / OEL), cross-contamination and cleaning, and approximate cost. Include the multi-company benchmarking studies of automated powder dispensing in pharma high-throughput experimentation (e.g. Bahr et al. 2018 and 2020) and any newer 2021-2026 evaluations, plus open-source or low-cost academic powder dispensers built for self-driving labs. Provide a comparison table and full citations with DOIs.

# Automated Milligram- and Gram-Scale Solid/Powder Dispensing in Pharmaceutical Research: A Technology Review

## 1. Introduction and Context

Automated powder dispensing remains a critical bottleneck in pharmaceutical high-throughput experimentation (HTE), self-driving laboratories (SDLs), and drug discovery workflows. The upstream step of weighing a solid into a vial—before dissolution and subsequent nanoliter-to-picoliter liquid dispensing onto microplates—demands milligram-to-gram accuracy, speed, and robustness across chemically and physically diverse powders. Solids present challenges that liquids do not: they may be light, fluffy, heavy, electrostatically charged, hygroscopic, or granular, and these physical property variations create substantial measurement and handling errors (nsouli2025advancingorganicchemistry pages 11-11). This review synthesizes the available literature on commercial, capsule-filling, conditioned-solid, and academic low-cost powder-dispensing approaches, with particular attention to their applicability for drug-discovery workflows and self-driving laboratories.

## 2. Major Commercial Gravimetric Platforms

### 2.1 Mettler Toledo Quantos / CHRONECT XPR

The Mettler Toledo Quantos is one of the most widely used automated powder dosing systems in pharmaceutical HTE. It employs a hopper-based module with spiral metal impellers that apply a rotary tapping motion to control powder flow onto an integrated analytical balance (christensen2021automationisntautomatic pages 3-6, jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 1-2). In independent benchmarking by Jiang et al. (2023), the Quantos was tested across thirteen chemically diverse solids at target doses of 20, 200, 500, and 1000 mg. At 200–1000 mg targets, many tractable powders achieved errors within approximately ±0.02–2% (e.g., −0.02% for Al₂O₃ at 1000 mg, 0.16% for NaNO₂ at 1000 mg, −0.01% for pectin at 1000 mg). However, at the 20 mg target, errors increased substantially: −6.00% for Al₂O₃, −5.04% for CaCO₃, −3.96% for NaNO₂, and −6.42% for granulated sugar (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 10-10). Complete dispensing failures (−100% error) occurred for compressible and hygroscopic materials including ammonium acetate and molecular sieve, attributed to clogging of the spatula outlet (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 10-10). Dispense times for sodium nitrite ranged from 285 ± 2 s at 20 mg down to 31 ± 3 s at 200 mg and 40 ± 4 s at 1000 mg (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 8-10). The overall average dispensing failure rate across all tested materials was 26.9% (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 10-11).

The CHRONECT XPR platform, developed by Axel Semrau in partnership with Mettler Toledo, integrates XPR balances with robotic dosing heads and vial logistics for fully automated workflows. It is identified alongside the newer Chemspeed platforms as capable of low- to sub-milligram dispensing, though independent accuracy data were not found in the retrieved literature (nsouli2025advancingorganicchemistry pages 11-11).

### 2.2 Chemspeed GDU-S SWILE, GDU-Pfd, FLEX, SWING, and Crystal Powderdose

Chemspeed Technologies offers a family of automated solid-dispensing platforms. The GDU-S SWILE is distinguished by its positive-displacement mechanism using a piston and glass capillary tube, combined with an internal measurement balance (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 1-2, christensen2021automationisntautomatic pages 3-6). This configuration enables dispensing of very small quantities and has been shown to be "highly effective in sub-milligram to low-milligram dispense quantities," including for sticky or oily solids that defeat passive hopper systems (christensen2021automationisntautomatic pages 3-6). In the foundational multi-company benchmarking study by Bahr et al. (2018), six different powders were dispensed over 3,240 times across three different platforms from 0.1 mg to 50 mg, and the Chemspeed GDU-S SWILE system was found to be "favorable for sub- to low mg dispensing of free-flowing or non-cohesive powders" (biyani2021advancementinorganic pages 4-7).

However, independent testing by Jiang et al. (2023) revealed that Chemspeed accuracy is highly material-dependent. At 1000 mg, errors ranged from −91.01% for Al₂O₃ (attributed to mechanical dispensing failures) and −0.41% for pectin to complete failure (−100%) for ammonium acetate (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 10-10). At 200 mg with all solids included, the average error spread was approximately 12% (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 8-10). Dispense times for NaNO₂ were 62 ± 23 s at 20 mg and 109–134 s at 200–1000 mg (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 8-10). The overall failure rate was 26.5% (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 10-11). Failures were attributed to problems with the opening/closing mechanism, abrasion of moving parts, and deliquescent materials adhering inside cartridges (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 8-10).

The Chemspeed SWING is described as more accurate for dispensing larger masses but not well suited for small target quantities, while the newer Chemspeed FLEX can measure low- to sub-milligram quantities (nsouli2025advancingorganicchemistry pages 11-11). The Chemspeed Crystal Powderdose is compatible with ChemBead formulations, achieving <5% RSD across 96-well formats when dispensing conditioned beads (tu2026sticktothe pages 4-5).

### 2.3 Unchained Labs (Freeslate) Junior and Big Kahuna

Unchained Labs platforms (successors to Freeslate/Symyx) are integrated HTE workstations combining solid handling, liquid handling, mixing, temperature control, filtration, and plate logistics. Their newer configurations offer low- to sub-milligram dispensing capability, though independent quantitative accuracy data were not found in the retrieved literature (tu2026sticktothe pages 4-5, nsouli2025advancingorganicchemistry pages 11-11). These systems, along with Chemspeed and Tecan, are identified as dominant vendors in the HTE automation space (christensen2022thedevelopmentand pages 62-68).

### 2.4 Other Commercial Vendors

Zinsser Analytic, Labman, Sartorius, Hamilton, Brooks/Titian, and Tecan offer various automated powder handling and liquid handling solutions. Their platforms are mentioned in the broader HTE literature as part of integrated automation ecosystems, but independent head-to-head powder dispensing benchmarking data comparable to the Bahr et al. studies were not identified for these specific vendors in the retrieved evidence.

## 3. Capsule Micro-Dosing Systems

### 3.1 Capsugel Xcelodose

The Xcelodose® system uses a vibratory "pepper-shaker" approach to fill capsules. A hopper fitted with a screen fine enough to prevent gravity-driven flow discharges powder into capsules via controlled vibration that reduces interparticle friction. The system handles doses from approximately 0.1 mg to several hundred milligrams and operates at approximately 600–1,200 capsules per hour (pinzon2012modellingofdosatora pages 34-38, pinzon2012modellingofdosator pages 34-38). A newer vibratory "pepper-pot" approach can precisely dose as little as 10 µg but is limited to approximately 600 capsules per hour (ding2021aqualityby pages 18-19). Dose-weight uniformity depends strongly on particle size, powder flow properties and bridging behavior, dispenser-head geometry (hole size and number), and the number of taps applied (pinzon2012modellingofdosatora pages 34-38). A stated advantage is that all powder enters the dosage form, producing zero powder waste (pinzon2012modellingofdosator pages 34-38). Dose-specific RSD values were not provided in the retrieved evidence, though acceptable uniformity for clinical trials was reported at 1–45 mg for favorable powder classes (faulhammer2014lowdosecapsulefilling pages 1-2).

### 3.2 3P Innovation Fill2Weigh

The Fill2Weigh system uses a gravimetric, vibratory micro-dosing approach with repeated weighing. Independent performance data were not available in the retrieved literature, though its operating principles are similar to the Xcelodose family.

## 4. Vibratory / Sieve-Chute Micro-Feeders

### 4.1 Khinast/Graz Micro-Feeder

Fathollahi et al. (2020) evaluated a high-precision low-dose micro-feeder developed at TU Graz. This piston/cartridge-based volumetric powder pump with a scraper can feed powders at rates as low as 1 g/h, with testing across a 1–20 g/h range (fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 11-12). It was designed to handle fine, cohesive, sticky, and low-density powders that defeat conventional feeders. However, tests with fine/cohesive API and spray-dried intermediate materials showed flow-rate deviations of 10–20% (fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 11-12), and related work reported variations of 4–20% depending on the material and feed rate (hou2024developmentofa pages 57-61). A key advantage is very low material consumption: tens of milliliters of powder suffice for testing, compared with 1–2 kg required by larger feeders, making it valuable for potent or expensive APIs in early development (fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 12-13).

## 5. Alternative Dispensing Strategies

### 5.1 ChemBeads (Coated-Bead Solid Dispensing)

ChemBeads, developed at AbbVie, represent a paradigm shift in solid dispensing for HTE. Solid reagents are dry-coated onto chemically inert glass beads using resonant acoustic mixing (RAM), which applies low-frequency, high-intensity acoustic energy to distribute the reagent uniformly over the bead surface through weak van der Waals interactions (tu2026sticktothe pages 3-4, tu2026sticktothe pages 2-3). Typical reagent loadings are 0.5–20% w/w, with approximately 5% being a versatile formulation that preserves flowability and homogeneity (tu2026sticktothe pages 2-3). Vibratory sieving after coating removes fines and aggregates to improve flow uniformity.

ChemBeads convert poorly flowing, cohesive, electrostatically charged native powders into uniform, free-flowing particles that can be handled volumetrically by robotic dispensing systems or manually using calibrated scoops (tu2026sticktothe pages 2-3). Automated dispensing achieves RSD values typically below 5% across 96-well formats (tu2026sticktothe pages 4-5), while a manual parallel bead dispenser demonstrates ±5% accuracy for 20 mg targets across 100 consecutive samples (tu2026sticktothe pages 9-10) and ±10% error for smaller quantities (gesmundo2023chembeadsenabledphotoredoxhighthroughput pages 2-3). The technology supports reactions at scales as low as approximately 400 nmol and can deliver 0.25–1 mg of material per well for nanomole-scale screening (tu2026sticktothe pages 7-8, tu2026sticktothe pages 10-12). ChemBeads are compatible with commercial dispensing platforms including Chemspeed Crystal Powderdose, Chemspeed SWILE, Mettler Toledo Quantos, and Unchained Labs Junior (tu2026sticktothe pages 4-5).

### 5.2 Dissolve-and-Dispense Stock-Solution Workaround

The dissolve-and-dispense approach prepares a known-concentration stock solution from the solid, then distributes it using established liquid-handling automation. This is attractive because liquid dispensing can be highly accurate, and acoustic droplet ejection (e.g., Labcyte Echo) enables nanoliter-scale downstream delivery. However, the approach is labor-intensive to prepare, unsuitable for poorly soluble compounds, may require toxic or volatile solvents, and can introduce concentration uncertainty from evaporation, adsorption, or precipitation (tu2026sticktothe pages 1-2, lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 1-3). These limitations make direct solid dispensing preferable when solvent addition is undesirable, material is scarce, solubility is limited, or the true solid mass must be delivered without bulk stock preparation (lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 1-3, lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 3-6).

### 5.3 STORMS: Stochastic Robotic Microsampling

STORMS (STOchastic Robotized MicroSampling), developed by Lisowski et al. (2026), represents a novel approach that deliberately abandons deterministic mass control in favor of stochastic sampling with post-dispensing weighing. A vacuum-assisted coring tool with interchangeable stainless-steel tubes (0.6 mm ID for ~0.1–1 mg; 1.5 mm ID for ~1–10 mg) samples powder from source vials, ejects it into pre-weighed glass capsules that are laser-sealed, and the exact mass is determined gravimetrically (lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 9-13, lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 3-6). Sub-milligram dispensing achieves an absolute standard deviation of approximately 0.06 mg, though practical precision is limited by the analytical balance's effective repeatability of about 0.2 mg under operating conditions (lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 13-15). Each capsule requires approximately 20–30 s, a four- to fivefold throughput improvement over deterministic dispensing (lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 13-15, lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 6-9). A critical finding is the Carr index threshold: passive sampling achieves approximately 96% success below a Carr index of 30, but drops to approximately 6% above that threshold; vacuum assistance improves performance for higher-Carr-index powders (lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 15-18, lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 13-15).

## 6. Open-Source and Low-Cost Academic Systems for Self-Driving Labs

### 6.1 Dual-Arm Robotic Dispenser (Cooper Group, University of Liverpool)

Jiang et al. (2023) demonstrated an autonomous biomimetic solid-dispensing system using a dual-arm robotic manipulator that manipulates ordinary spatulas, vials, and hoppers over an analytical balance with fuzzy-logic correction. The system achieved dispensing accuracy as low as 2 mg and, at 200 mg targets with non-challenging solids, demonstrated a mean error of 0.07% with 0.56% standard deviation—outperforming both Quantos and Chemspeed on these materials (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 8-10). However, dispense times were substantially longer: 239–552 s per dose across 20–1000 mg targets (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 8-10). The overall failure rate was 23.1% (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 10-11). The system can handle some abrasive and coarse materials that damage dedicated dosing heads, but fails with compressible, highly deliquescent, and sticky powders (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 10-11, jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 1-2).

### 6.2 SALSA 3D-Printed Archimedes Screw Doser

Zhang et al. (2026) developed SALSA, a low-cost automated salt solubility screening module for battery electrolytes that features a 3D-printed Archimedes screw solid doser. The motor-driven screw, housed inside a 3D-printed PLA tube, conveys and dispenses powder with closed-loop feedback from a balance positioned beneath the receiving vial. The system dispenses at least 0.3 g of solid, with the balance providing 0.1 mg resolution (zhang2026salsaalowcost pages 2-3). Interchangeable, customized 3D-printed doser heads accommodate different powder types: a standard funnel for NaNO₃ and a wider-neck, shorter-exit funnel for finer Li₂SO₄ to reduce clogging (zhang2026salsaalowcost pages 5-6). The system is explicitly designed as a low-cost alternative to expensive commercial solid dispensers (zhang2026salsaalowcost pages 2-3).

### 6.3 Self-Driving Tableting DataFactory

Abbas et al. (2025/2026) described an integrated platform for tablet formulation development using automated powder dosing (via a DEC Group FlexPTS volumetric doser), tablet compression, and performance testing within a Bayesian optimization loop. The dosing unit adjusts powder chamber volume via a piston position, collects powder by vacuum, and discharges with compressed air (abbas2025acceleratedmedicinesdevelopment pages 23-26). This illustrates the broader trend toward integrating powder dispensing into closed-loop SDL workflows for pharmaceutical development.

## 7. Dependence on Powder Properties

Across all platforms, dispensing performance is strongly dependent on powder physical properties. Key factors include:

- **Cohesion and flowability**: Cohesive powders with small particles (<50 µm, especially <20 µm) show greater interparticle forces, reduced flowability, and increased weight variability (hou2024developmentofa pages 64-67, faulhammer2014lowdosecapsulefilling pages 4-5). Powders with Carr index >30 (or equivalently, Hausner ratio >1.43) approach a threshold where passive dispensing mechanisms achieve very poor success rates (lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 15-18, lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 13-15).
- **Electrostatic charge**: Should be minimized through appropriate construction materials, as it can interfere with powder movement and contribute to adhesion or blockage (hou2024developmentofa pages 64-67).
- **Hygroscopicity**: Moisture promotes liquid bridges, surface tension effects, and increased cohesiveness, while also potentially altering bulk density and causing particle softening (hou2024developmentofa pages 64-67).
- **Particle shape**: Irregular shapes increase surface area, cohesive forces, mechanical interlocking, and friction; spherical or rounded particles generally improve flow (hou2024developmentofa pages 64-67).
- **Compressibility**: Highly compressible solids can clog spatula outlets and piston mechanisms, leading to complete dispensing failure (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 10-10).
- **Abrasiveness**: Can damage moving parts in both SWILE and Quantos systems (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 10-11).

Hausner ratios of 1.12–1.18 are associated with free-flowing powders suitable for automated dispensing, while higher values indicate increasing difficulty (ekenlebie2015pharmaceuticalprocessoptimisation pages 69-75). The Faulhammer et al. (2014) study of low-dose capsule filling demonstrated that RSD could not be simply correlated with dosing volume, but lower fill weights generally produced higher RSD values, and very fine, low-density, cohesive powders (group II) had significantly more difficulty meeting specifications (faulhammer2014lowdosecapsulefilling pages 9-10, faulhammer2014lowdosecapsulefilling pages 1-2).

## 8. Containment and Cross-Contamination

Published benchmarking studies of automated powder dispensers focus on accuracy and throughput rather than containment performance (OEB/OEL classifications). No independently verified OEB or OEL ratings for any of the reviewed platforms were found in the retrieved literature. In practice, containment for potent APIs is achieved through engineering controls such as enclosed gloveboxes, dedicated/disposable dosing heads, laminar airflow, and validated cleaning procedures. The Xcelodose system is specifically designed for clinical-trial capsule filling with high material recovery and enclosed loading for potent APIs (pinzon2012modellingofdosatora pages 34-38, ding2021aqualityby pages 18-19). STORMS's disposable sealed glass capsules inherently reduce cross-contamination risk (lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 1-3). ChemBead formulations reduce loose airborne dust during dosing, though coating preparation still requires neat-reagent handling (tu2026sticktothe pages 4-5). Cross-contamination between compounds in automated systems requires cleaning validation of all product-contact surfaces, which varies by platform architecture.

## 9. Approximate Cost

Pricing for commercial platforms is proprietary and not reported in published benchmarking studies. Based on market context: Mettler Toledo Quantos modules are estimated at US$30–60k, while complete integrated Chemspeed, Unchained Labs, and CHRONECT platforms represent six-figure capital investments (christensen2022thedevelopmentand pages 62-68, jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 1-2). ChemBead dispensers using manual calibrated scoops are low-cost, while RAM coating equipment and automated bead dispensers add substantial cost (tu2026sticktothe pages 4-5). Academic systems such as the SALSA 3D-printed Archimedes screw doser are explicitly designed as very low-cost alternatives (zhang2026salsaalowcost pages 2-3), though the exact bill of materials was not reported.
